Mr. H. B. MORPHY (North Perth) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 66, to amend the Railway Act. He said:
The purpose of the Bill is to amend paragraph (e) of clause 34 of section 2 of the Railway Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 37. The Act as it stands includes, under the head of ''working expenditure" of railways ''(e) all rates, taxes, insurance and compensation for accident or losses." The Bill which I ask leave to introduce

extends the language of paragraph (e) to make it read in this way:
(e) all rates, taxes, insurance and compensation for accident or losses, including any such compensation payable under the provisions of any Act of the Parliament of Canada or of any provincial legislature providing for the payment of compensation to workingmen for injuries or in respect of industrial diseases.
The object of the Bill is to extend to the workingman who is injured the privilege of having his claim come under section 141 of the Railway Act in the same way as rates, taxes, insurance and compensation for accident or losses. It will give the claim of a workman who may suffer accident and loss priority as against a mortgage or bonding deed covering the railway's assets in the same way as rates, taxes and insurance now have a prior claim. This will bring the Railway Act into line with the new legislation of the province of Ontario dealing with compensation to workmen for injuries sustained. It is merely to extend the law as it stands, and it seems to be an amendment that is necessary in the case of a railway company which may be insolvent and unable to pay claims for losses. In such a case the workman's claim will have priority over a mortgage deed the same as the other elements now in the law have priority.
Motion agree.d to, and Bill read the first time.

Hon. W, J. ROCHE (Minister of Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 67, to amend the Yukon Placer Mining Act. He said: An Order in Council was passed on the 28th October by which all those who had enlisted for service in the war had their mining rights protected until six months after the proclamation of peace. Inasmuch as this did not apply to those acquiring rights under the Placer Mining Act in the Yukon, the Commissioner of the Yukon was instructed by the department shortly after the passing of the Order in Council that it was the intention of the department to have the same privileges extended to those who had acquired rights of a similar character in the Yukon under the Placer Mining Act. As the Placer Mining Act could not be amended to this effect by Order in Council, this amendment is introduced.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
1.	Bathing (by use of ordinary bath tubs) is imperative as a sanitary regulation of the prison and is carried out weekly by the officer in charge of the ward as a matter of routine, without special orders from anyone. If the officer neglected the duty, he would be reported by his superior officer to the warden. Except in very" rare cases, the convicts comply willingly and appreciate the opportunity. Occasionally, however, a refractory lunatic refuses to comply, in which case the bath is enforced by the officers-due care and precautions being taken to prevent the convict from injuring himself or the officers in charge.
2.	The warden is unable to find any one on the staff of the penitentiary who has any knowledge of tubbing having been used except as before described. The following are the statutory declarations of officers who are still on the staff of the prison and who have been, from time to time, in charge of the insane ward:
Dominion of Canada, province of Ontario, county of Frontenac, to wit:
In the matter of the inquiry regarding the alleged " tubbing '' of the insane at the insane ward of Kingston penitentiary.
I,	Patrick J. Madden, of the city of Kingston,

in the county of Frontenac, guard, do solemnly declare that I was in charge of the insane ward from September 3, 1907, to August 31, 1911, and from September 13, 1911, to September 26, 1911.
During that time there were filthy prisoners who refused to bathe. There was a strap placed round the body of the prisoner and two for the hands and one for the feet. This strap was used for the protection of the convict and the officers. These straps were only used for refractory convicts while bathing and for no other purpose. The water used was ordinary bath water.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true, and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of " The Canada Evidence Act, 1893."
(Sgd.) P. J. Madden.
Declared before me at the Kingston penitentiary in the county of Frontenac this 23rd day of February, A.D. 1915.
(Sgd.) J. Russell Foster.

I,	Charles H. Gray, of the city of Kingston, in the county of Prontenac, guard, do solemnly declare that I was on duty in the insane ward from April 1, 1912, to May 25, 1912.

I,	Robert E. Aiken, of the city of Kingston, in the county of Frontenac, guard, do solemnly declare that I have been in charge of the insane ward since November 11, 1913.

He said: My object in presenting this motion is not to ask for information a-s to

why there was a camp at Valeartier for the first contingent. The necessity for having a camp there has not been made clear to me nor, I believe, to the general public. If a camp was needed, Petawawa was available for the purpose, but the contingent which is now in course of preparation is being assembled neither at Valeartier nor at Petawawa; more properly, perhaps, the men are being assembled at the different stations throughout the Dominion where recruiting is going on. I believe it would have been better if the same policy had been adopted in respect of the first contingent. But what I wish particularly to bring to the attention of the Minister of Militia to-day is that many of the owners of land who were disposessed for the establishment of Valeartier camp -have not yet been paid. I understand that the camp comprises nearly ten thousand acres, and that between forty and fifty men were dispossessed. These men, practically all farmers, were not in circumstances of affluence, and each one needed the crop which he was then expecting to raise, and, of course, the price of bis land upon expropriation. On August 28, the following notice was served upon one of the men so dispossessed -I understand that a similar notice was served on all.
From Lt.-Col. Wm. McBain.
Quebec, Que.,
To Mr. Michael Holton.
Dear Sir:
I have been instructed by -the Department of Militia and Defence to notify you herewith that it is their intention to expropriate the land held by you in Valeartier and described as parts of Cad. Nos 54, 68, 67, 68 and list Cad. No. 71, on the official plan for the parish of St. Gabriel de Valeartier containing in all 240 acres.
I have been further instructed to notify you that it is the intention of the department to take immediate possession of the above described land and to offer you in full and complete settlement therefor the sum of $4,800. If this offer is not accepted by you within thirty days of the date of this notice, proceedings in expropriation will be commenced.
Kindly take notice of the above and govern yourself accordingly.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) Wm. McBain, Authorized agent of the Department of Militia and Defence.
Who was Mr. McBain? For my part I do not know, nor did any of those to whom these letters were addressed. He was not connected with the Department of Militia. He styled himself colonel; I understand that he suddenly rose from a rank of obscurity to be a full-fledged colonel of the first rank. The management of the camp at Valeartier had been placed at first in the

.hands of Sir William Price, a well-known business man of the city of Quebec and a former member of this House, a man holding the highest reputation for business ability and integrity of his character. Why Sir William Price was not continued in the agency of the Department of Militia is not known to me, but I believe that the change does not conduce to the public interest. I think there would have been less complaint than there has been if Sir William Price had been continued as agent of the department instead of Colonel McBain. I do not wish to reflect on Mr. McBain; I do not know him; but I do know Sir William Price very well, and, not knowing Mr. McBain and knowing Sir William Price as I do, and as everybody in this House does, I believe the change was not calculated to promote the public service. Be this as it may, the one fact I make complaint of is this: I have been informed-I have no special information except that which I received by correspondence-that though these men were dispossessed of their lands in the month of August last, yet, with the exception of one or two, these owners, some forty or fifty in number, have not yet received the money to which they were entitled. There may have been some dispute as to price. This was not unnatural. But I desire to represent to my hon. friend that in view of the circumstances an extra effort should have been made to give these people ample satisfaction. These men had their property invaded just at the time when their crop was ready. Some of them could not gather anything of their crop, and some of them are reduced, I will not day to penury, but certainly to stringent circumstances, in consequence of the delay. And, so far as I know, no effort has been made to have these men paid. I understand that the matter has been referred to the Department of Justice. That is to say, all these men have to go to law in order to get their money. If their claim has been put into the hands of the Department of Justice, that department cannot proceed except by due course of law; these forty or fifty owners, suddenly despoiled of their property, will have to go to the court to get the value of their land and also of their crop. I make this motion simply to have the information from the minister. Charges have been made as to the management of the camp. I make no charge; I simply ask for information.

The leader of the Opposition has dwelt upon the necessity of Valcartier camp; but he says he will discuss that at some other time. I am willing to oblige him and will reply to his criticism of the camp at Valcartier at some other time. But, inasmuch as he went out of his way to discuss it a little, I may point out that the camp at Valcartier stands unique in the history of the world as having produced the best shooting regiment that ever wore a uniform. The object in getting the force assembled at Valcartier- war being a game of shooting-was to give the boys an opportunity to learn practically how to hit the bull's eye. They succeeded; and let me say, without disrespect to the second contingent, which is made up of a lot of as fine boys as ever gathered in any part of the world, that it will take them six or eight weeks' actual practice at the targets before they will be in the same class -I refer to rifle shooting alone-with the boys who sailed on the 1st of October.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition asks, who is Colonel McBain? May I tell him?
Certainly.

Col. McBain is a descendant, a great-grandson, of an officer who stood beside Wolfe on the Plains of Abraham. Colonel McBain's ancestors ever since 1759-nearly as long as the ancestors of the leader of the Opposition- have lived at Valcartier, on the very spot where this camp was erected. Col. McBain is a gentleman of whom the city of Quebec and his home district are very proud. Col. McBain is a gentleman who struck out into western Canada years ago and who by honest business industry has amassed a fortune. Col. McBain is a gentleman who, when the call to arms came, volunteered for any position to go to the front. Col. McBain is a gentleman who has given his time and his services freely to the Canadian Government, 1 believe without any remuneration-I am not aware that he has accepted any; and in some ways I know he has refused it-in order to perfect the boys for service at the front.
The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) wants to know why Sir William Price was not given the position. Sir William Price is another distinguished gentleman of whom the people of Quebec and the people of Canada are proud. He also volunteered his services and refused to accept

What is the date of the memorandum?
Major General HUGHES; It was given to me to-day; I do not know when it was prepared. Every effort has been made to bring about a settlement, and, more than that, we instructed each of the valuators to give a fair valuation. My right hon, friend may not know this locality well, but the McBain family is one of the oldest in Quebec. Every effort was made to induce these people to accept the fairest possible valuation, and instructions were given to give compensation because the people were being turned out. When some of the people demurred at taking what was considered a good, fair valuation, we used every effort to bring about a settlement, and I understood that in every instance the offer had been accepted until, through some manoeuvring, the spirit got abroad among them to hold for higher prices.
Motion agreed to.

That, in the opinion of this House, the circumstances arising out of the present war are such as to justify the Government of Canada in exercising supreme control over the quantity

and destiny of our food exports, thereby regulating the prices at which bread, meat and other food products shall be sold for home consumption. while at the same time directing that our surplus food exports should only reach British or friendly countries.
He said: The resolution standing in my name is one which I deem of great importance at the present time. It has no political significance, so far as I am concerned. It has appeared to me that for some months past it was the duty of those in charge of the Government of the country to keep a very good eye upon the food supply of the Dominion of Canada, and also to assist in every way*possible the Mother Country iri the tremendous struggle in which she is now engaged. I am aware that the principle contained in the resolution upsets to a certain extent what has been deemed proper economic law, that is, that the law of supply and demand regulates the prices of all commodities.
At the same time this war has upset a great many business axioms, has upset the calculations of many political economists and has brought to our attention the fact that a world-wide war is not dealt with by ordinary means nor controlled by ordinary circumstances. Supply and demand as a rule is a safe criterion for the fixing of prices of commodities. As far as I have been able to judge, Canada is the only country at present at war that has not given more or less consideration to this very important question. Very early in the war the Government of the sister dominion of Australia, that great Commonwealth, which is also a large producer of food, took possession of all supplies of wheat and arbitrarily fixed the price at $1.25 per bushel. That was done in one of the leanest years that Australia has seen in a long time. Their wheat crop was comparatively a failure. The supplies for nome consumption were away below the requirements of that great country. New Zealand is in very much the same position and has been obliged tp appeal to Canada for its supplies.
Wheat, of course, is not the only item to be considered in a resolution such as this.
I have purposely drawn the resolution as broadly as possible. You will notice that the wording used only asks that the House concur in the opinion that the Government is justified in controlling both the quantity and destination of food exports. There may be those, and no doubt there are a number,' who disagree with the first proposition but I believe that in this House it will be found that no one will disagree with the second proposition in regard to the destination of our food supplies. Surely the people of Canada who are the holders of greater or lesser quantities of food products can have no doubt in their minds that the exportation of these food supplies should be directed towards the Mother Country, friendly peoples and allies who are fighting with her to-day for the great principles that we believe are involved in the present war. Therefore, I assume that there will be no exception taken by any hon. member of the House to the proposition that the export of food supplies from Canada should be entirely to British and friendly countries. I have put in the word " friendly " out of deference to the opinions of some who may not agree with me, but for my part I would have preferred to have confined the resolution to British countries entirely because I believe that in the present crisis all our available food supplies are required by the Mother Country and the sister dominions.
Moreover, those who have studied the condition of this question and have followed it fairly closely, as I have for the past few months, must be forced to the conclusion that we are in rather a critical position at the present time, and in asking the House to give some attention to this very important question I am only asking it to do what has been done in the government circles of the various countries that are engaged in the war at the present time. Only this morning you will notice by the press that Air. Lioyd George has been dealing with the matter and I shall have occasion to refer to that a little later on and also that taere was held in Trafalgar Square yesterday a large gathering of the labouring element protesting against the high prices of food and pointing out that it was necessary in the interests of the workingman that the food supply should be immediately regulated and that prices, if necessary, should be set by the Government. That is a proposition that it may be difficult to carry out in such a country as the motherland. On the 11th of February the British House of Commons passed an entire day in discussing this very important question and further, at the close of the debate, after an amendment had been moved by one of the labour leaders, another day was set for the continuation of the debate. Mr. Asquith, it is true, stated that food prices could not be regulated in the United Kingdom with beneficial results. Let me point out that the conditions in Great Britain are exactly the opposite of the conditions that we have in Canada. Great Britain is a food-importing country; even in normal times the food

supply has to be almost entirely brought from outside sources. Britain's problem is to get enough food to come into the country. Canada's problem is to prevent too much food going out of the country. One perhaps is uncontrollable, but there is no one who can say that the other is uncontrollable, and it appears to me that the crisis at which we have about arrived, and I think more than arrived, is such as to demand that the subject should receive the very best thought and attention of the Government. The wheat supply, particularly of Canada, is in very narrow compass. Probably not 10 per cent of the wheat grown is at present in the hands of the farmers. Far be it from me to propound any proposition that is going to rob the farmer of his legitimate profits. The farmer has had to take too low prices for many years past for his wheat there is not a bit of doubt about that. Personally if the farmer can get $1.50 or $2 for his wheat in so far as the matter of trade is concerned I am perfectly satisfied, but coming from an industrial constituency where there are 7,000 employed in the ordinary way, and where, owing to an ihdustrial stagnation the like of which we have never found before in my time, 2,000 or more have been out of work almost the entire winter, with wheat, bread, oatmeal, meats and various products of the farm bringing prices that have rarely been experienced in the years gone by-
When you speak of 10 per cent being in the hands of farmers, do you include seed wheat or only the quantity for sale?

I estimate that there is not more than 10 per cent in the hands of farmers for sale. I shall deal with the seed question a little later on, because that is an important factor to he considered at this particular time.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he would reduce the price of wheat to the farmer for the purpose of benefiting his own constituency?

I have not made any such statement, and if my hon. friend will wait until my argument is finished I think he will not arrive at that conclusion. I am quite aware that some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House may not agree with my proposition, but at the same time I have the courage of my convictions, and I believe that not only in Canada but in every

one of the countries at war this is a real live question that has to be dealt with on its merits. And, while my hon. friend from Brandon (Sir James Aikins) may think that the farmer is justified in getting $2 or $2.50 per bushel for his wheat, under war conditions, I am not going to say whether or not that should be the price fixed; I have not in my resolution named any price, nor do I propose naming any price to which wheat, and meat, and the food products consumed by the working men should be limited. I point out that while the price of securities of every kind, industrial transportation, insurance, railways, has been going down, and down, and down, in the last six months, on the other hand we have seen the necessaries of life of the workingman rising steadily and rapidly. I have a mass of statistics here, a part of which I can only place before the House, which show that the present condition of the wheat supply of Canada wants very careful watching. I believe that in the next six weeks we shall see a squeeze greater than anything we have yet seen. The visible supply of wheat in Canada is shrinking rapidly day by day, until it is estimated that the visible supply, as I am informed by responsible authority, is down to about
18,000,000 bushels, and that is disappearing at. a very rapid rate. That has come about in Canada on top of a world shortage. The United States is the only country ip the world which had a good crop last year, the world supply being about four hundred million bushels short of the crop of the previous year. We all heard the discussion that took place about two weeks ago, in reference to the seed grain proposition, in the interests of the West, and on that occasion we were told by some hon. gentlemen that thousands	of farmers in
the West have not even the seed with which to plant their land this spring, so that, if this statement be correct, the bulk of the farmers are now buyers rather than sellers, of wheat. I am glad to know that this Government has had the foresight to place aside a large sum of money for this purpose, and that they have already made purchases of a considerable quantity of wheat to supply this seed shortage. The great squeeze, as I see it, will come in seeding time this year. Canadians are now the greatest wheat-consuming people in the world, bar none, for while the people of the United States consume annually about five bushels per head of the population, Canada consumes between six and seven bushels. Taking our population at from 7,000,000 to

7.500.000,	in round figures, our requirements for the bread of the people of this country are between 45,000,000 and 50,000,000 bushels of wheat per annum, and in addition to that we will have, in the very near future, to supply seed wheat for a very large aj'ea. It may be said that should a shortage take place we can import from outside, but from what countries can we hope to get the supply we need? The United States is to-day practically the only country that has'a large visible supply that is available. The world's supply has been cornered and speculators, in Chicago largely, have been setting the price of wheat for the world during the last few months. The United States surplus, and it was a very large surplus, has been disappearing at the rate of eight million bushels per week. Great Britain, France and Italy have been compelled to purchase immense supplies from the United ^States. Italy is not even yet at war, but the Italian Government has taken the precaution to buy
40.000.	000 bushels of wheat from the United States, as the following despatch shows:
Rome, February 28,-Provisions made by the Government to supply Italy with wheat pending the next harvest were defended by the Minister of Agriculture, Signor Cavasola, in a speech yesterday before the Chamber of Deputies. He declared special missions representing the military commissariat bad made enormous purchases in the United States and Argentina, although the largest quantities had been made in New York and Chicago. The total contracted for abroad, Signor Cavasola said, was 13,500,000 quintals, (40,500,000 bushels), which will be divided between several of the largest cities as distributing stations.
About one-third of the amount contracted for already has arrived in Italy. The Minister of Agriculture declared that in view of the precautions taken by the Government a wheat famine would be impossible, because the supply provided for would be ample to last until after the Italian harvest.
After the speech of Signor Cavasola, the Socialists provoked a political test vote and were defeated, 314 to 44.
This proves that even these countries which are outside of the war zone are compelled to take extraordinary measures for the preservation of their food supply. I think you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that nothing could be more deplorable, than to see the success which has attended the efforts of the Allies thus far set at naught by a food shortage which may cause very serious trouble in the Motherland. I quote from a speech delivered by Lloyd George in Bangor, Wales, on the 28th instant:
The Chancellor of the Exchequer, David Lloyd George, made a pointed reference to the United States in a speech here today.
" If Germany is triumphant over this country," he said, " she would be practically dictator. of the world, and where," he asked, 34
" could we then look to a chivalrous country to protect us-to America?"
If countries like France and Russia, with huge armies, and we, with the most powerful navy in the world, could not face this terrible machine, how could America step in? It would be more than America could do to defend herself in her own continent. America is unready more than we were."
The chancellor then took up the liquor industrial questions.
" The Government has wide powers to deal with the drink question, and it means to use them," he declared. He said a small minority of the workmen employed in the armament factories had refused to work a full week because of the lure of drink.
" The government would use its powers discreetly and in a spirit of moderation, Mr. Lloyd George asserted, but " fearlessly." He was sure the public would support whatever action was taken and allow no indulgence of this kind to interfere with the country's prospects in the war.
" The war," he said, " is to be won or lost by the engineers. We need men but we need arms more than men and every day of delay is full of peril to the country. For one reason or another we do not get the assistance we have a right to expect from our workshops. Industrial differences are inevitable, but we cannot afford them now.
" It is intolerable that the lives of Britons should he imperilled for the sake of a farthing an hour. During war, governments should have the power of settling differences so that work shall go on. If men are entitled to more money the government should give it. I do not believe the parties involved will refuse to comply with the urgent command of the government that there should be no delay."
Expressing confidence in the outcome of the war, the chancellor said the people of the country hardly realized yet the importance of the struggle in which they were engaged and warned them that victory could not he won without a long struggle. He declared that while England had enrolled the largest volunteer army ever gathered in any country or in any century it ought to be larger still.
There is also in this paper an article headed: '"Protest the food prices." In it the socialists draw attention to the fact that the Government has not done everything possible to safeguard the food supply of the workingman. There is danger to-day in the Motherland in regard to the food supply. I appeal to the House and to the people of Canada: Is it right or wise for any set of men to endanger the success of the allied forces for the sake of some monetary advantage to the individual citizen? The question simmers down practically to that. We are to-day facing a crisis such as has never before been experienced by the British Empire or by the world. If by a restrictive policy on the prices of our food products we cause any delay in turning out munitions of war and other army supplies, which are just as important in their way as are the men at the front, would it not be to the detriment of our cause, which I am sure
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend from Brandon (Sir James Aikins,) who is an expert lawyer, though I do not know that he knows much more about wheat than I do, says, so it is, or something to that effect. But I have sufficient confidence in my own opinions to tell the hon. member that though he objects I still hold my opinions as strongly as he holds his, and I think I have just as much right to hold them. I believe, even though the hon. member may not agree with me, that the people of this country have a very keen eye on the situation as it now exists, and it is a situation that, I think, cannot be given too much consideration at the present moment. It would be a thousand pities if Canada, the granary of the British Empire, as we have called it, should fail at this critical moment. There is danger of its failing to do what is expected of it in the food supply. The resolution I have placed on the Order Paper is drawn broadly and lays down in very general terms the possibilities that may arise, and asks this House if it does not justify the Government in taking into its hands this position that may require dealing with. I do not ask my hon. friend to subscribe to any particular price for wheat. I do ' not set any price; I do not think it is in my province to do that. If it is thought that $1.50 a bushel is a proper price for wheat, all right; if $2 a bushel even is thought better, all right. I can remember as a boy when wheat was as high as $2.50 a bushel, and it may go to that again. But what I would point out is that there are many workingmen in this country who cannot afford to pa-y this price for their bread unless they have a corresponding increase in their wages. Now, the workman has been up against two propositions-first that his wages are dropping at the present time and that he has been very short of work in all the industrial centres; and second he has been asked higher prices for bread and for the products of the farm that go upon his table than at any time for years past. It may be said that I represent a few manufacturers. I repudiate that before it is said. While I may get ten or fifteen manufacturers to vote for me, I am here by the votes of the workingmen of the city of Brantford. I am here to represent the interests of these men and not the miller or L4i
the speculator, or the man who endeavours to comer the food of the people.
With permission, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he has made any calculation of the amount of wheat which has gone out of the hands of the farmer into the hands of the miller?
I have some figures here dealing with that subject, but not of very recent date. The quantity in the farmers' hands, according to my figures, is about 8,000,000 bushels at present.

Ijow much in the
hands of the millers?	_

I have shown that the millers and speculators have bought about ninety per cent of the crop, which was put at 158,000,000 bushels. That would leave about 15,000,000 bushels in the hands of the farmers according to that calculation.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but the point I wish to make is this: Undoubtedly the millers bought a great deal of this wheat during the months of December and January for somewhere about a dollar a bushel. Now, the way in which this question affects the workingman is through the price of flour. What I want find out, if possible, is what proportion of the wheat of the three Prairie Provinces was bought from the farmer at a price of $1 a bushel or less, and whether there is good reason for flour going to the price to which it has gone.

I am afraid I could
not give authentic figures on that point. I have stated that I believe that ninety per cent of the wheat of the country has passed from the hands of the farmer into the hands of the miller, who is more or less of a speculator. I d(^ not think the price the millers have paid for wheat justifies the present prices of flour. I think the miller has made a very large amount. Judging by the figure at which milling stocks are selling and the profits the millers are said to be making, it looks to me as if the millers have the big end of the stick. I do not think it would be wise to endeavour to curtail the operations of the millers in the interests of the people, but I think it reasonable to point out that the millers, being a very small percentage of the people of Canada, should not expect to make out of a world-wide disaster a large personal profit, amounting in some cases almost to a fortune. I have here a

clipping from the Ottawa Free Press, a journal which I do not often quote with approval. 1 may be excused for quoting it now inasmuch as this article comes from a Conservative paper, the Montreal Star, something which deals with the question my hon. friend has asked:
With the conditions indicating that the larger milling companies in Canada are likely to have one of the biggest years they have ever known, many local interests are already figuring on the bonuses the companies will he able to pay over and above regular dividends.
The principal companies have only gone five months of their regular fiscal year, but it is admitted that whether peace comes eo-morrow or in a year from now, conditions are going to favour the Canadian companies for a couple of years at least, and on this account the companies are bound to make a very good showing, even though profits are not anything as large as some people have been figuring.
In the case of one of the local companies, it is stated that earnings this year may run not far from 50 per cent on the common stock, -while in the case of some of the still larger .concerns, it would not he surprising to see earnings of from 20 to 25 per cent, even when the statements have been worked out on a conservative basis.
From this it will be seen that the millers have struck a very prosperous time, though most of,the country is suffering in a financial way. As I have said, we have seen all our securities sinking. Every industrial company, every transportation company, every joint stock company of any kind has seen its stock go down, and down, and perhaps has found that stock unsaleable even at a fraction of the original price. Exchanges all over the world were closed on account of the war for several months, and those that did business did it on a limited scale and at prices almost unheard of in, the history of the companies affected. Even Canadian Pacific railway stocks fell from 280 to 155. Almost all industrial companies, except, perhaps, the milling companies, have felt the pressure of the disastrous conditions which are the result of the w'ar.
In the face of all these circumstances, the prices of food supplies have risen. Wheat at $1.50 a bushel in ordinary times would not hit anybody so very hard. I have said more than once in this House and throughout the country that wheat should never sell at less than $1 a bushel. I believe that the farmer either of the West or of the East can not afford to raise it at less than that price, and if the Government should think it wise to establish the price of wheat at $1.50 or $1.75 a bushel, I would make no protest. But what - I want the House to decide is this: has the time come .jvhen the 
export of the staff of life produced in Canada should be controlled? Is the amount of the visible supply a justification for the Government's saying that when a certain price is reached they will step in? I propound this question in all seriousness. I have shown that the visible supply is lower than it has been for a long time, and, in the face of the most extraordinary demands from all parts of the world, is rapidly passing away. On the other hand, sources of wheat supply that were formerly available are now entirely shut off. Great Britain has always looked to Russia for a large supply of the staff of life, and the conditions to-day are such that not a boat has been able to get away from Russia, either to the north or to the south, for many months. Hon. gentlemen may say that the Dardanelles are very soon to be open, but Mr. Asquith himself anticipates that liberal supplies will not come from that source before June-and before June a great squeeze will come in this country. It is true that the allied fleets of Britain and France are operating upon the forts of the Dardanelles, and we are told by the press that they have succeeded in silencing three or four of the outer fortifications. But it is yet a long way to Constantinople, and it is a still longer way to Odessa. For my part I think that those who are anticipating a food supply from Odessa will be pretty hungry if they have not substantial reserves nearer at hand and more easily available. These fortifications may fall, but other difficulties will then present themselves. If the hostile shores are held by the enemy, there will be difficulties of mines in narrow channels, and of torpedo boats; under these conditions is it reasonable to expect that merchant ships will be passing from Odessa to Great Britain in the very near future? I may be pessimistic, but I think not. Then where is Great Britain to obtain her food supply in the future, and particularly during the next few months? Argentina, so far as I know, is the only source of supply outside of the United States, and I have told you that the United States is shipping at the rate of 8,000,000 or 9,000,000 bushels a week. Practically the world supply of this important cereal, the staff of life for nearly all peoples, must come from the United States and Canada. We hoped that in time of stress we in Canada would be able to turn out from 150,000,000 to 200,000,000 bushels of wheat; unfortunately this year we did not do anything like as well as we did in 1913. This we all deplore. While I do not wish to be unduly pessimistic, I say in all seriousness that

the present crisis may soon require action by some department of government, probably the Department of Trade and Commerce. I am glad to know that we have at the head of that department a shrewd man of business, a man upon whom we may depend to do the right thing at the right time.
I think it would be reassuring for him to know that this House has provided legislation which he may put into force when it is necessary to take definite steps to conserve our food supply before it is too late.
I cannot conceive of any greater calamity to the people of Canada than that of overexportation of food products at this serious time. The Allies need those exportations.
I have before me a report with regard to the American wheat supply which I think I should place upon Hansard. For this report I am indebted to Mr. John Bunnell of the Chicago Board of Trade, an ex-Canadian. He is an expert in such matters, and is a recognized authority in that great centre of wheat production and distribution. This is the report:
The 1914 wheat crop of the United States was estimated to be 891,000,000 bushels. The estimated surplus carried over from the 1913 crop was about 76,000,000 bushels. There was, therefore, a total available supply of 967,000,000 bushels, and as the normal per capita consumption of wheat in the United States is about 5.3 bushels, 520,000,000 bushels should meet our normal domestic requirements for food. In addition, 90,000,000 bushels are required annually for seeding;	610,000,000
bushels, therefore, should supply the normal domestic demand.
It will be noted that 90,000,000 bushels are required for seeding, purposes only in the United States; therefore the figures which I gave some time ago are quite in accord with the assumption that we would require in this country 20 or 25 per cent of that amount. The report goes on:
This would leave a surplus of 357,000,000 bushels. Of this surplus about 210,000,000 bushels were exported by January 30.
About two-thirds of the amount they had to spare.
This left 147,000,000 bushels, or 40,000,000 bushels more than our average annual export for the past five years, for export between February 1 and the appearance of the new crop, or for carrying over into the next crop year. The amount is sufficient to permit the exportation of nearly 1,000,000 bushels a day until July 1, before which time the new crop will begin to be available. This is about the average recent exportation.
I have already said that they are exceeding the export of 1,000,000 bushels a day; if they continue to export at that rate they will entirely consume their surplus before
July, which is a time entirely unfavourable to the securing of wheat in large quantities
The large demand for our wheat arises from the fact that there was an estimated world's shortage of over 400,000,000 bushels, outside of the United States;
A shortage of 400,000,000 ibushels in the world's supply, coming on top of a world war !
-from the fact that the Russian exportable surplus of 100,000,000 bushels is not available generally and from the fact that the belligerent nations are eager to secure food supplies. If it were not for these things we would be discussing ways and means of disposing of our surplus food products. As has been stated, the new American crop will begin to appear before July. The Argentine crop is now coming on the market. It is estimated that from that source there will be available 100,000,000 bushels. A surplus of 75,000,000 bushels or more from India will be available in May and June. The increase in the fall sown wheat acreage of the United States in 1914 was 11.1 per cent, or over 4,000,000 acres; in fhe| northern hemisphere generally the increase in the wheat zone shows an increase of from three to thirty-three per cent, as follows:

But suppose a shortage in wheat should develop in the next three months, what would .he the situation? There is a great surplus in other food crops in the United States, a number of which can be used as substitutes. Wheat does not constitute more than 12 per cent of the normal diet, about the same as poultry and eggs.
This corroborates what I have said, that there is a very large shortage in the world's supply, and the demands are of such an unusual character that all calculations of the past may be upset by the facts .of the present that the warring nations are more or less nervous, day by day, as to the requirements of their people and as to the food supply. It is not necessary for me to recount to you the horrors which at present exist in some of these countries in order that you may realize wihat a shortage of food would mean to vast numbers of people. In Belgium we have to-day practically 7,000,000 people who are dependent on the outside world for their entire food supply. We are told that it requires 80,000 tons per week of food to keep 7,000,000 people of Belgium from starvation. They

know what war is. We in Canada fortunately, up to the present time, have scarcely realized what war is and we have not realized that we are personally called upon to make the sacrifices necessary for our cause to triumph. I think that every one of us should be prepared to make all necessary sacrifices for the success of the cause. It may be that some of us will be called upon to sacrifice flesh and blood. That is the highest sacrifice that man-can make for man, and I am glad to say that there has been a spontaneity of response throughout the Dominion of Canada where the call has gone forth:	" Your King and country
need you." But that is only part of the battle. We have to send the men to the front, we have to send them equipped, and then we have to supply them with the munitions of war and with the food required to carry on the war satisfactorily. To-day the greatest problem in Britain is to maintain the supply of armaments, shot and shell and rifles and cannons and all those engines of destruction that are required to meet an enemy whose every man is equipped from head to heel, in a way that no army in the world has ever before been equipped, ready, the moment the war bugle sounded, to march forward in the ranks of war to meet any enemy in the gate.
Lloyd George has said, in the speech from which I have quoted, that they are fighting in such a way as no war machine has ever fought in the history of the world, and we are called upon to make all necessary sacrifices in order that our cause may triumph. I want to put it to the members of this House, I want to appeal to their patriotism if mot to their pockets, is it not the part of Canadians, is it not the part of any Britishers to be ready to sacrifice not only their flesh and blood if necessary, but also what is far less of a pang, some of the profits which might go into our pockets as the result of a squeeze which would mean tremendous pressure on others. My hon. friend only laughs. I am afraid that all my shafts are lost on him, but I feel that, *whether he agrees with me or not, he as a patriotic man must say that we are called upon to make some personal sacrifice. Is that not right? He will not agree with me to that extent. I know that my friend from Brandon (Sir James Aikins) is a highly philanthropic citizen and that he has sometimes, if not converted souls, made a good attempt to appear on religious platforms as a man who was attempting to save
[Mr. Cockshutt.J
souls, and I appeal to him now,
5 p.m. I appeal to his Christian charity, I appeal to him as a man who draws out his soul to the hungry and is ready to satisfy the afflicted soul. These are not my words, and I think he will know where they come from. I ask him if he will not draw out the bowels of his compassion and say that $1.50 or $1.75 or even $2 is enough for wheat to sell at. He is still dumb. However, without asking my hon. friend to subscribe to the proposition I am making, I think I can fairly ask the members of this House to let their bowels of compassion be moved for souls who are in want, that those who need the food of which we have, to limited extent, a surplus, may get the benefit of our surplus. But we cannot afford to feed even those who are worse off than ourselves if it is done to the detriment of our own people. While charity begins at home, we want to exercise just'as much of it as we can to those of our kith and kin over the seas; and while I say that the resolution which I have moved may not appeal to all in one respect, that is, in the desire to limit our exports, I believe I can appear to all that the exporting of those food supplies should be limited to British and friendly countries. I would prefer that it should go only to British countries, because I think it is the duty of a man to look after his own household first, to see that his own wife and children are fed; in other words to care for the people of his own nation, his own kith and kin, to whom he is bound by all that is Christian and all that is charitable, to provide for the wants of those who are suffering within the borders of his own country. I believe I shall carry the House with me in that respect, that our food supplies which do go abroad should go only to British and not foreign countries.
A return is in my hand, sessional paper No. 120, showing the countries to which food supplies have been exported since the month of August last; and while I shall not weary you with the fish and the cheese and apples ard minor articles ti nt go to replenishing the table of the workingman, I am going to uraw your attention to the fact that in regard to wheat and flour and some other cereals we are in the humiliating position, to a certain extent, of having fed the enemy while many of our own people were not receiving food in a quantity or at a price that is desirable. That, I think, is something that should be rectified. I find in a return I asked for that we exported wheat to several non-British

countries. The order was for a return showing whether any exportations of foodstuffs have been made since August last to European countries other than the United Kingdom, France and Belgium. In response to that order I have a statement showing that 167,626 bushels went to Gibraltar, and 40,000 bushels to Denmark. It may be said that as far as Gibraltar is concerned, we were feeding the British garrison, and very likely we were; but as far as Denmark is concerned that cannot be said. But it is to the matter of flour more particularly that I want to draw the attention of the House. Since August last we exported flour to the following countries:

We should not have sold one barrel to Germany while our own people needed it. I do not know what Greece wanted with all that flour. I am afraid that she did not use it herself. What did Norway do with 120,954 barrels of flour? I fear that some of this flour has been sent to furnish the sinew's of w'ar to our enemies. We have made mistakes up to date with regard to the exports of flour, but oats is just as important a commodity as flour, as far as the success of our arms is concerned, because there is a tremendous demand for the oats of this country to feed the war horses that are at present fighting our battles in northern France and Belgium. The position of the oat market is just as important as that of the wheat market in that respect, and we must be just as careful in regard to it. We want to see to it that no further mistakes be made in sending food supplies to the enemy or in sending them to those countries that may be friendly with the enemy and which allow these supplies to be sent from their borders into the country tlhat is fighting against the armies of the Allies. I think that has been done; I am afraid it has been done.
I know that there is a disposition to blame the bakers of Canada for the inordinate rise in the price of bread. I am not familiar with the baking industry, but I have had a document sent to me by the bakers who repudiate the assertion entirely and who make the statement that they have gone on furnishing bread at a price that the
present price of flour does not at all justify, that now they are practically at the end of their resources so far as flour that was laid in early in the w'ar is concerned, and that very material advances must be made in all kinds of bread, cake and other things which the bakers furnish from day to day to the houses of workingmen. If that is the case it is a very serious matter, and it is certainly deserving of the consideration of this House because, after all is said and done, fully half of the population of the Dominion is resident in cities- We have close upon 700,000 men at the present time working in the industries of Canada. All of these are dependent for the staff of life pretty much on the bakers' product and I therefore appeal to this House to see that no injustice is done to any of those concerned in debating this question. I am making no imputation agaiqst the good faith of all our citizens. Far be it from me. I have the very highest respect for all classes of our citizens. I believe we have a splendid citizenship in Canada. I am endeavouring to direct the attention of the House to what I conceive to be one of the most important resolutions that will come before it at this session of Parliament: I am asking hon. gentlemen to say that in the judgment of this House the Government would be justified in controlling the amount of foodstuffs to be exported and the destination to which they should go. I am asking you to place no particular price on any product but I believe that when the resources are held in this country that of itself will be a regulator of the prices and that it will result in maintaining a constant supply of our breadsituffs and all those items that go upon the table of the workingman.
What I have said in regard to bread-stuffs applies in a smaller measure to all kinds of products, to cereals and all those items of daily use that go upon the table of the working-man. They all require consideration at the present time and I ask you, as a fair proposition, to see to it that we in Canada, largely a food-producing country, shall not allow ourselves to be impoverished by overexportation until we have taken care of the food requirements of our own people and of the supply of seed grain to those who are presently to go upon the land to sow the crops for the coming year. I am in entire accord with the Government in furnishing seed grain to the farmers. I think it was a wise move, but that of itself may affect the the situation at present existing somewhat acutely. I therefore have much pleasure

in moving the resolution which stands in my name. I thought it was the intention of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) not the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Barnard) to second the resolution, although I do not think it makes very much difference. I offer the resolution believing that in doing so I am bringing to the attention of the House and the country a question that demands their very best consideration, and whether hon. gentlemen agree with me or not, I ask them to discuss the question free from any political bias or anything of that kind because I have no thought of that in my own mind at the present time and it has no tearing whatever upon the introduo tion of this resolution. I ask simply that this question be viewed upon its merits and I can only say again that I make this proposition believing that it is a wise and just one and that its adoption is in the best interests of the people of Canada and of the British Empire whose cause we have so very much at heart.

Being a farmer and representing a farming community, I desire to say a few words upon this very important question. I would like to have a little more information on the resolution that has been laid on the table. I would like to know if the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt) is trying to get after the farmer or who it is he trying to hit. I believe that if the adoption of this proposition should affect the farmer it would inflict a great injustice upon him. I admit that at the present time the farmer is receiving a fair price for his product, but at the same time I do not believe .that the price that he is receiving represents more than a good living profit. I wonder if the hon. member for Brantford lost much sleep when the farmer was receiving a starvation price for his butter, eggs and other products. I am a farmer and I know that the farmer at the present time is selling his cattle and his hogs at a price that does not pay him, considering the high cost of everything he is using. I believe that the consumer is paying too high a price for his foodstuffs, over and above the price the farmer gets. I know that in August and September last buyers paid $9.75 per cwt. for hogs, and $9.00 per cwt. for cattle, while to-day they are only [laying $7.25 for hogs on the Toronto market and a correspondingly less price for cattle than theypaid in August, and yet they are asking exactly the same price for their beef and pork as they did last fall, when they were paying two cents per pound

more for live stock. There is something wrong there, and if the Government wants to obtain power to get after those fellows. I for one shall approve of their doing so. If the farmer alone is to be detrimentally affected by such action as is now proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Coekshutt) I believe it would be most unjust. For the last few months there have been people going around the country advocating patriotism and increased production, but if you are going to adopt any legislation in this Parliament which will be injurious to the farmer, how are you going to get increased production. For my part I believe that the farmer requires protection just as well as the manufacturer. I wonder how the hon. member for Brantford would like it if the Government brought in a Bill to stop the shipping of ploughs to the other side, I think he would object to that most strongly. I believe we should not be selfish; I believe we should co-operate, one with the other; I believe we should allow the farmer to live. The farmer is the backbone of this country, and we must have protection for him. A great deal is said nowadays about the high cost of living, and I might perhaps give my experience in that respect. I am a farmer, but I am also a merchant, and I think I am able to deny the statement that the cost of living has greatly increased of recent years. I worked behind the counter in my store for thirty-seven years, and I know from personal experience that thirty-five years ago, with a few exceptions, the cost of the necessaries of life was higher then than it is to-day. Thirty-five years ago I sold tea at seventy-five cents a pound, and I am selling as good tea to-day at forty cents a pound; thirty-five years ago I sold coffee at thirty cents a pound, and I am selling as good coffee to-day at twenty-five cents a pound. I believe that as a whole the price of drygoods is lower now than it was say thirty years ago. That, of course, depends on whether the people are willing to use the same class of drygoods to-day that they did then. If people were willing to use the same drygoods to-day as they did thirty years ago, they could buy them just as cheaply; but nowadays the/ want style, and they have to pay for it. Thirty years ago the mothers on the farm would spin the yarn and the home weaver would weave the cloth; I wore these goods myself and I was content with them; but to-day the boys and girls are not satisfied with that. It is the way the people live to-day

that makes the cost mount up. About thirty-five years ago I remember selling six pounds of granulated sugar for a dollar, while to-day I am selling twelve and fourteen pounds for a dollar. Of course, the cost of living, especially in large cities, is high, and that is brought about largely by the high rents, which are the result of the good times we have been having. In the good times in the past, speculation ran high and rents ran up. Where twenty-five years ago an ordinary man could rent a house for ten or fifteen or twenty dollars a month, to-day he is paying thirty or forty or fifty dollars. We must place the responsibility for that on speculation. I did not expect this resolution to be brought up to-day, and I was not prepared to speak upon it; but it having come before the House, I felt that it was my duty to say a few words on behalf of the farmers. Those who live in the cities imagine that the farmer has an easy time of it, but I am in a position to know about that, and I feel satisfied that the farmer, even in view of the high price he is rceiving to-day, has the short end of it, and that he is not making the money he ought to make to recompense him for his hard work.

It was not my intention to have spoken on this resolution, nor did I think I would until after I suggested a question which perhaps to my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) was somewhat unfortunate. He drew particular attention to the hon. member for Brandon, when that member felt carried away by that inspired patriotic peroration of the hon. gentleman, pointing out how the people of this country should sacrifice themselves for their homes and for the Empire. He apparently misunderstood my disposition and turned his particular laudations to myself. While he was thus considering the member for Brandon, my thought was turned to see how his enthusiastic patriotism was given effect to by the resolution he placed before the House and now being considered, limiting the market and price of agricultural products. By this resolution he asked that some portion of this community should make sacrifices, and that portion of the community which he selects to make the sacrifice is the farmer. I can tell my hon. friend that the farmers of this country, and particularly the West, are willing to make and have made splendid sacrifices for Canada and the Empire. Thousands of the best men, sons of farmers, and farmers themselves, young, vigorous, intelligent and
industrious, having ample opportunity for the development of their life at home, have sacrificed their peaceful pursuits and comforts and are now manning the trenches in a foreign land fighting our Empire's enemy.
But that is not the - sacrifice which the hon. member for Brantford desires the farmers of this country for the love of it to make. When we consider this resolution we find that the sacrifice he demands of them is a sacrifice for the benefit of other people in this land, and particularly for the benefit of the manufacturers and the benefit of the employees of those manufacturers. In my view, Mr. Speaker, if sacrifices are to be made, they surely should be made by those who hitherto have had the benefit of the services of their workmen, and who have received advantages from them.
If any one is called upon to make sacrifices, it should not be those who have constantly paid tribute to the manufacturers of my hon. friend's constituency and the eastern part of Canada. As I understand this resolution its purpose is that the price may he reduced to the agricultural producer so that the consumer may receive the benefit of that reduction. Therefore the sacrifice that the farmers are being asked to make is for the benefit of other classes in Canada.
There are two great producing classes in our country-the agriculturists and the manufacturers. Who should receive particular attention? Certainly those whose production is the natural and not the artificial production of a country. If we look at the returns for the year 1913, we shall find that the value of the agricultural exports was either three or four times greater than the value of the manufacturers' exports. As Canada is	primarily	an agricultural [DOT]
country, the agriculturists, if any protection of the people is given, should first receive that protection. I presume that any economic policy that is wise and sane for one class of producers should be wise and sane for the other class of producers.	We have very frequently seen
pamphlets sent out by the Department of Trade and Commerce-the minister for which deserves all the commendation which the hon. member for Brantford has given him-setting forth the wider market that the Government is attempting to create. For whom in particular? For the manufacturers. Seldom do we see any such pamphlet for wider markets for the fanner. When that subject was before the House, instead of giving wider markets for wheat.

I must first of all congratulate the hon. member for Brandon (Sir James Aikins) on at length having arrived at a very sane idea of the doctrine of protection in so far as the agriculturists of this country are concerned. If my hon. friend had been of the same view with respect to markets for the farmers of this country last session, and the session before, and, in fact, for the past three or four years, we might have had free wheat to-day for the farmers of western Canada. I do not wish to impugn the motives of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) in bringing this resolution to the attention of the House. I have heard the hon. member on previous occasions get very close to the same doctrine as he has promulgated here to-day, namely, the fixing of the price of foodstuffs. It is quite true that he would not venture to suggest what the value of a bushel of wheat would be. I believe on one occasion, some two or three years ago, he said that wheat should never sell for more than $1 a bushel.

Mr. COCKSHUTT; I never made that statement.
You got very close to it to-day.
Your imagination is carrying you away.

The sole purpose of his resolution is to control the price of wheat, which ithe bon. member himself has said, produces the staff of life which feeds all the people of this country. This is a most peculiar time in the history of Canada for a man to advocate in this House the control of the price of the main product of our farmers. During the past few years I have heard gentlemen of the type of my hon. friend advocating that the farmers of this country should go into mixed farming. When the farmer had about come to the conclusion that mixed farming was a good thing, the war came in August last, and immediately my hon. friend and his friends advocate that people should produce more. And now, I suppose, we have the climax of this campaign of " Patriotism and Production " in the speech of my hon. friend, advocating that the farmer should not be paid more than a certain price per bushel for his wheat. I submit that the hon. gentleman has started at the wrong end of this question. I am informed and believe-and perhaps my hon. friend has the information- that the millers of Canada are manufacturing flour out of wheat bought three or four months ago at prices not exceeding a dollar a bushel at Fort William. I know, and hon. members of this House know, that during October and even September-because our harvest was early last year-and during November, there was no dollar wheat in western Canada. It was the exception if the man got 98 cents or 99 cents a bushel, and from that were deducted transportation charges to Fort William. The farmer got for his wheat on an average from 80 cents to 90 cents a bushel. And I am informed, that the millers fortified themselves with a large supply of wheat which did not cost them. $1.25 a bushel or anything like it. And yet flour is selling at $8.75 a barrel.
There is another reason why the hon. gentleman has started at the wrong end of the question. He knows, as does every other member of this House, that for many years past the Canadian miller has been selling his flour in the markets of the world at a less price than that at which he sold it to the consumer in Canada. What is going to be the result of raising a question
of this kind? I agree with the hon. member for Brandon (Sir James Aikins) that the agricultural business is the maip industry in Canada. To increase the prosperity of this country, to get men on the land in the East and in the West, and to get larger acreage in crops and to get more agriculturists on the land, a campaign of " Patriotism and Production " is undertaken. I saw some figures the other day with respect to the population centering in the cities. While the rural population increased from 1900 to 1910 by half a million people, the population of the cities increased by almost a million and a quarter-or almost two and a half times the increase of the rural population. Of course, the cities are always attractive to a large number of people, but the main attraction has been the comparatively high wages that were paid there, especially by the manufacturers. The manufacturers did not raise wages for philanthropic reasons. They have acted in this matter the same as they have in relation to the doctrine of protection; it was an absolutely selfish proposition. They were forced to raise the wages of their employees because the cost of living has so greatly increased within the last fifteen years. The effect, of course, was to increase the wages of all city employees. The farmer could not compete with these prices, and so the farmer's hired men and the farmer's son went to the city. And now my hon. friend proposes that the price of the farmer's principal product should be curtailed. I would suggest to him, as the hon. member for Brandon said, that he might consider advantageously some reduction in the cost of agricultural implements in western Canada. Let me give an instance that came under my own notice a short time ago, one the facts of which I am ready to substantiate at any time the hon. gentleman wishes. A certain man bought an engine gang plough. I ascertained these facts at Carnduff. I learned that the machine was quoted there at a certain figure. But this man crossed the-line into Sherwood, in North Dakota, and bought the plough there at such a price that though he paid about $100 duty on bringing it across the line, he saved $80 or $90 on the transaction. Does the hon. gentleman dispute that? That was a Canadian-made plough, one that had paid duty on going into the United States. Yet, though it had paid that duty and though it had to pay another duty on being brought back into Canada, the purchaser saved the amount that I have named. It was one of the agricultural implements manufactured by those philanthropic gentlemen of On-

tario, manufactured and sold abroad at 20 per cent less than they charge for it in Canada.
The hon. gentleman wishes to control the price of the product of the farmer, but. at the same time he is arranging that his friends the Government of the day should increase the duty on the implements that the farmer uses, and on everything that the farmer consumes. That is the policy of my hon. friend. I would like to know what the Government think of that policy. Is it in favour of the policy of curtailing the price of all the foodstuff that the farmer produces and to enhance the price of all that the farmer uses?
As I have said, what we most of all require in western Canada, and I believe in the whole of Canada, is to get men on the land. Canada is primarily an agricultural country. We have prided ourselves on that for many years past. But immigration has practically ceased during the last six months, and it has been declining, like our revenue, for eighteen months past. If we are to get the farmers on the land to carry out the "patriotism and production" policy that we have heard so much about, how can any reasonable man defend the position that the price of the main product of the farmer's labour shall be fixed? I say, I believe that the majority of the House will agree that the farmer should be allowed the price for his products fixed by the open competition of the world.

My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) has said a good deal in former years on questions similar to this,' but formerly he argued on the other side. To-day he is very anxious to protect the workingman, not only of his own constituency, but of the whole of Canada. From what the hon. gentleman says, one would suppose that the workingmen of Canada ate bread and nothing else. I am prepared to favour the proposition of the hon. gentleman if he will ask the Government to regulate also the prices of everything that comes on the workingman's table. But I suppose he will not accept that, for otherwise he might be'blackballed by the association of which he is a member. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman has changed from the position which he occupied in former years in this argument. For my part, I have always said that the farmers did not get enough for the goods they grow, yet the consumers always had to pay too much. The hon. gentleman can hardly
[Mr. W. M. Martin.!
deny that. There is a middleman somewhere-there are many of them, and my hon. friend is one. I would ask him in two words also to make some sacrifice, and would ask the trust of which, I assume, he is a member, to make some sacrifices. And I would say to the trust of the millers, which is really one of the biggest in Canada, and which has paid dividends on watered stocks of so many million dollars, that surely they also could do something for the country at the present time. My hon. friend may say that they are not paying any dividends this year. They are very sorry that they cannot pay any dividends, but I may remind hon. gentlemen that when I brought this question up in the House on a previous occasion it was plainly stated that these people were paying no dividends except on common stock. I may tell my hon. friend that I will second his proposition on the condition that the regulation or restriction of prices shall apply to every article of foodstuffs that goes on the workman's table. I may say, too, that I shall be willing to make some sacrifice if the interests with which my hon. friend is connected are willing to make one also.

The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Coek-shutt) spoke of Canada as being the granary of the Empire; I think it will be admitted that vrestern Canada is really the granary of the British Empire. The hon. gentleman proposes to make provision for the regulation of prices of foodstuffs, which would include the larger number of the products of western Canada. Farming in western Canada has not been profitable; that was established only last year by the report of the commissio'n appointed by the government of the province of Saskatchewan to inquire into farming conditions. That was due largely to the prices received for the grain which the farmers produced. This year, when exceptional conditions prevail and there is a prospect of the farmer obtaining a good price for his wheat, the hon. member for Brantford comes Along with a proposition to restrict the prices within certain limits and practically to wipe out the first opportunity for making a profit that the western farmer has had for a great many years.
What will be the effect of the proposed changes in the tariff upon the farmers of western Canada? The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) argues that the price of the protected article goes up just to the extent to which the tariff is increased.

I have before me substantial proof that since the Government increased the protection afforded to certain agricultural implements, the price of agricultural implements has been	raised, and	the new	prices	arenow	in effect.	I	will	quote	the
statement, not of a politician, but of a gentleman who is engaged in the implement business in the city of Winnipeg.
I have here a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press of Tuesday, February 23, containing the report of an interview with Mr. H. W. Hutchinson, vice-president and managing director of the John Deere Plough Company. Mr. Hutchinson argues that the entire tariff, in so far as it affects tillage implements used upon the farms, imposes a burden upon the farmer of western Canada. We have been advocating, as Mr. Hutchinson points out, increased production, but production can only be brought about by utilizing tillage implements, and upon these the Government, under its proposed tariff arrangements, is putting an extra tax. Let me read what Mr. Hutchinson says in that regard:
The prairie farmers will, of course, be called on to pay the duty. We have been already notified by Canadian manufacturers that prices will be increased to us and we have already begun to prepare a new price list for the sale of our commodities. On every walking plough tin re will be an increase in the price paid of from $1 to $2; on every sulky plough an increase of $4 ; on every drill an increase of ?5.
Do these increases apply to ploughs made in the United States or to ploughs made in Canada?
Mr. Hutchinson says, "We have already been notified by Canadian manufacturers."
So far as our firm is concerned, there is no truth in that report of an increase. It has been decided by the firm that prices shall remain just as they have been.

I presume that the hon. gentleman, who has dissociated himself from the agricultural implement business within the last couple of years, is probably more familiar with these conditions than I am, but I shall wait until I receive word from some of the farmers in western Canada who are buying the implements before assuming that Mr. Hutchinson's statement is incorrect. Mr. Hutchinson proceeds to enumerate the increases:
On every gang plough an increase of $6 ; on every wagon an increase of ?7, and on every disc plough a nincrease of ?8, with similar advances in the prices to the farmer Of all kindred tools.
Then there follows a lengthy interview with Mr. Hutchinson, in which he says that the tariff increases are discouraging to the farmers of western Canada. In view of the fact that the prices of these articles are to be increased, I submit that even if the prices of grain in eastern Canada to-day rise higher than they ever have been in the past, the additional prices which the farmer will have to pay for the articles which are given additional protection under the tariff changes introduced at this session of Parliament, will reduce his profit and take away from the benefit of the increased price he receives for his products.
The hon. member for Brantford takes a patriotic view of the situation. I wish to tell my hon. friend-not as a boast, but as a statement of fact-that there i& no more patriotic part of Canada than the West; that there is no more patriotic citizenship in this country than that which is found in the farmers of western Canada. I have had the pleasure of attending a great many patriotic meetings in my own constituency, a constituency largely populated by men and women who come from the republic to the south. Those men and women have been interesting themselves in the promotion of every patriotic object, and are prepared to make sacrifices on behalf of Canada until the war is over and victory is proclaimed on behalf of the Allies. They are prepared to make sacrifices on behalf of patriotic enterprises, and they are prepared, if need be, to sacrifice their sons to the Empire. In my constituency a squadron of mounted rifles has just been raised to goto the front with the third contingent, and in that squadron there are six officers, each one of them a native horn American citizen who has only recently become a naturalized citizen of Canada. Any one who is under the impression that our new citizens are not true Canadians lias been entertaining' mistaken ideas.
I believe that this war itself has developed a stronger Canadian citizenship than we have ever had in the past. It has proven the metal, it has proven and established the loyalty, of the people who have gone into western Canada; and they are prepared to make their contributions, but they are not prepared to be limited in the price which may be offered to them for the products of the soil, and then have to pay increased prices for the articles which they use. My hon. friend in his resolution says:
While at the same time directing that our surplus food exports should only reach British or friendly countries.

My hon. friend surely has kept in touch with Britain's attitude during this war. He knows that to-day it,faas been declared that no food of any kind will be allowed to go into Germany or any other country opposed to the Allies on account of the attitude of Germany and the countries allied with her. Why is that? Wie can get food'products to the Allies and the friendly countries because of the existence of a great power within the British Empire, and this resolution, I maintain, is not necessary in that regard, because all our surplus products are more than likely to go to the countries to which we want them to go-to Great Britain and to the allied nations.	-
