My hon. friend the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), has brought forward a resolution that I do not think he can expect this House to approve of. At the present time my hon. friend is engaged in supporting a measure before this House which is to add very heavy burdens, not only to.the farmers in the West, but to the farmers all over Canada. It is bad enough when you hit any class of the people one blow, but in this resolution that my hon. friend presents to the House he proposes to give the farmer the double-cross and hit him at both ends. He adds to the price of his machinery, adds to the price of everything that goes to produce wheat and if, on one particular occasion or in one particular year out of a great many years, the products of the farm are high in price my hon. friend wants the Government to step in and fix the price. I acknowledge that farmers are getting good, high prices for their products at the present time.
Some of them.
Well, most of them.
Pork is very low.

Some of the farmers have got good prices and because they happened to have got good prices my hon. friend comes forward and wants to have the prices fixed by the Government. I think the hon. member for Brantford is beginning to learn something, and that is that high protection does not always protect or benefit the interests that he is so anxious to have benefited. Surely the proposition of the Government to increase the price of manufactured goods should be sufficient for my

hon. friend who represents a manufacturing constituency-a	constituency composed
nearly altogether of manufacturers and artisans. If that proposition worked out as they would lead us to believe, the artisans of that constituency should be benefited, but according to the hon. member for Brantford they are not being benefited, he finds the prices of products too high and he comes to this Government and wants to have them regulated.
We have heard a great deal of late years about getting the people back to the land. What I am particularly concerned about is endeavouring to keep the people on the land that we have on the land at the present time. People have been leaving the land steadily and now, when you are placing heavier burdens than ever before on the backs of the men who are trying to make a living on the land, how does any one expect, how does the hon. member for Brantford expect, that we will be able to get more people back to the land or even that we will be able to keep the men on the land who are there now? My hon. friend, with a show of patriotic fervour, declared that we should make sacrifices. What sacrifices are his constituents making? What sacrifices are the manufacturers making under the legislation that is before Parliament to-day? I heard one manufacturer from Montreal make the statement-and he made it knowing what he was talking about-that the added duties that are proposed at the present session would mean 5 per cent additional profit to the manufacturers. These are not my words, these are the words of a practical manufacturer. If these added duties, of which the farmer will have to bear the biggest part, will enable the manufacturer to made an additional 5 per cent profit, I would like to ask my hon. friend where the sacrifice comes in. I have never been able to see any sacrifice that the manufacturer has ever made. The vice-president of the Manufacturers' Association said that they would have to grin and bear the extra taxes, but I notice what the Ottawa Citizen said chiefly grin, and, it i= a case of grin on the part of the manufacturer it he can make five per cent extra money.
I hope the hon. member for Brantford will not succeed in having liis resolution carried into effect, because it would mean that the farmer, in addition to the extra burden that he is going to be called upon to bear, wouid be precluded from taking advantage of good

prices for his wheat, or his cattle, or anything else in the way of food that he produces, at any time that it happened that the prices were extra heavy. I would like to ask my hon. friend if Great Britain has asked for any such action on the part of the Government of this country. I do not believe she has. The hon. member fo'-Brandon (Sir James Aikins) has pointed out the statement, in a despatch to the press to-night, that Great Britain had food enough on hand for the next twelve months. I do not think there is much suffering from the lack of food, and I think it would be a step in the wrong direction absolutely if the Government were to place any restrictions whatever in the way of the farmer getting the very best prices lie can. My hon. friend from Brantford, only a year or two ago, supported very heartily a proposition in this House to prevent the farmer from selling his wheat on the other part of the line if he could get a better price for it. He could not see that there would be any advantage in that whatever, but if my hon. friend from Brantford refused to allow the farmer to sell his wheat in the best market that happened to be available, and that best market was across the line, and if he is supporting the policy of added burdens to the farmer in producing that wheat, surely he does not want to give him a third welt and to say: We must prevent the farmer from getting the market value of his wheat because that is going to make the cost of living too high for my constituents. That is exactly what he says-the cost of living is going to be too high. My hon. friend will find out that when he undertakes to legislate upon all these matters he just gets them going from bad to ivorse, and that it would be far more in the interests of his constituents, as well as in the interests of the whole Dominion, if they would leave matters as they are and not add any greater burdens to the farmer and not give any greater concessions to the manufacturers. He would then find that the cost of living for his constituents would not go up nearly as fast, and that they would be in a much better position than if the Government were to accede to their request anu put a limit on the prices that the farmer could get for his product. If anything were	going	to be	done	in that
line, now is not the time to do it. I can hardly think that the Government would entertain this idea for a moment; but if it were going to be done at all, the time'would be before the grain has largely
passed out of the farmers' hands-it is not altogether out of their hands, but a very considerable portion of it is-and into the hands of the great milling concerns. However, I am not at all alarmed that the Prime Minister will do anything of the-kind asked for by this resolution. It does not seem to me it is a motion in the right direction and I do not think the members on his own side of the House will accord the hon. member very much support.

One of the ideas of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) in proposing his motion appears to be that most of the wheat in Canada has been secured by the millers-and other speculators at a low price, and' that these men are taking advantage of the war conditions to charge consumers an inordinate profit, and he seems to think that in some way or other this resolution if carried would regulate the price to the consumer. I do not think it would have that effect. The motion says:
That, in the opinion of this House, the circumstances arising out of the present war are such as to justify the Government of Canada in exercising supreme control over the quantity and destiny of our food exports, thereby regulating the prices at which bread, meat and other food products shall be sold for home consumption, while at the same time directing that our surplus food exports should only reach British or friendly countries.
According to the proclamation issued by Great Britain and the Allies, the surplus products that Canada has to ship will only reach Great Britain and other friendly countries, and, therefore, that part of the resolution is not necessary. And if, by reason of that fact, you control the price of the home grain then there is no part of the resolution that is necessary. There is no doubt that the millers and other speculators are charging a very high price for flour at the present time, and if they have bought this wheat at a low figure before the price advanced, there is no doubt whatever but they are taking advantage of present conditions, and whether they should be allowed to do that is a point worthy of consideration. This is a combine-ridden country-
Say that again.

My hon. friend
wishes me to repeat that, but everybody knows it who wishes to know it, and therefore it is not necessary for me to repeat. We have combines to raise the price of food and other products, and if they can be smashed, it would be a good thing for Can-

ada. There are men in this country-we all know it-who are taking advantage of the war conditions to make fortunes of thousands and tens of thousands of dollars out of the food and other products they are selling to the people of this country, and to the Government of this country, which is another name for the people. If the bon. member for Brantford had moved a resolution asking for a parliamentary committee to find out who the guilty parties are, and to try to prevent these practices, I for one would support him. The resolution of the hon. member in its present form would be innocuous and useless were it adopted. Something should be done to prevent the people from being fleeced, and to prevent the designs of the cormorants who are trying to fatten upon the people at this particular time, by taking advantage of the patriotism and loyalty and devotion of the people. These men think that perhaps their raids upon the treasury and upon the people of Canada may pass unnoticed, but we know them and they should be brought to book. Action in this direction taken as speedily as possible and before Parliament prorogues would be in the best interests of the country and of the Empire. If my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) had proceeded along that line, I am sure he would have got support in this House, from independent members at all events, and perhaps some one may yet move in that direction. That is the view I take of this resolution.

I
am only going to detain the House for a moment to loou on this question from the point of view of increasing production throughout Canada, especially farm production, both in the East and in the West. Having regard to the present situation, if I were asked to suggest something to improve the condition of the farmer of the West in the matter of increased production of foodstuffs, I would suggest the adoption of a policy by the Government to valorize or stabilize the price of the forthcoming wheat crop. 1 would be quite willing to see the Government make a price for the first and seconu grades of the coming year's wheat crop, somewhere in the neighbourhood of SI.40 or $1.50 per bushel. Tnat would enable the farmer to hold the wheat until they got at least that price for it. If a better price were obtainable they would get the benefit. Py the Government valorizing and stabilizing the price of wheat, the farmer would get what he does not get

to-day, namely, the large amount which the miller takes away from him. The bulk of the wheat that has been raised by the farmers of our western country has gone into flour, and that flour has been sold, as nearly as I can make out, at a price which should have netted the farmer from $1.30 to $1.50 a bushel. There are always new ideas in economics, ana the suggestion has been made, and I think it is -worthy of consideration having regard to the present conditions, that the Government of Canada could well afford to stabilize the price of the coming crop at least at $1.30 a bushel. If we cannot do that, there are other things we can do to help the farmer. There are two things that could be done in that direction and the Government is doing one of them now in increasing the storage capacity in the West so that the farmer can keep his wheat until such time as the miller wants it, and thus secure a better price. A widespread system of storage throughout the West will no doubt help in that direction. Then we should have a banking system in this country that w-ould enable the farmer to carry his wheat, so that he would not be compelled to sell it as wn as the crop is reaped, If the farmer could store his wheat and if he [DOT]could have a banking accommodation that would help him to carry his wheat, we would accomplish what ought to be accomplished, namely, not a reduction in the price of wheat in this country, but the increasing of the price in every possible way, or at least the enabling of the farmer to get the price which he is entitled to get for his wheat. The Government should enter upon a policy of valorizing the price of wheat, especially of the higher grades; but we certainly can at least provide storage for the wheat and furnish a banking system that will enable the farmer to carry his crop until such time as he can sell it at a fair price. If we had those facilities to offer to the western farmers, farmers would flock to the West and settle, there, and we would see the West thrive as it has never thrived before.
Freight rates also have a bearing upon this question, and there may be relief in that direction. Parliament should find a way to improve the condition of the western farmer and to enable him to get the best possible price for his wheat. If we do that, we shall increase our production in a most surprising way; we shall bring prosperity again to the West, and we shall see a new and greater West in the near future.

Mr: D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton) : I have followed with a great deal of interest the speech of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). I am sure, whatever any one else may have said about the speech of my hon. friend, that he has at least brought a good deal of live information and reliable statistics to the notice of the House. The subject to which he has drawn our attention is .certainly one of the greatest possible importance. During this discussion the hon. member for Brantford has been criticised for propounding a policy. It certainly cannot be said that the hon. gentleman has been propounding any policy. As I understood him, he was propounding a way in which to deal with an urgent condition of things brought about by the extraordinary state of the country at the present time. The resolution is perhaps not as well drafted as it might have been. As I read it, there is only one categorical assertion in it, namely:
That, in the opinion of this House, the circumstances arising out of the present war are such as to justify the Government of Canada in exercising supreme control over the quantity and destiny of our food exports.
There cannot be any objection to the resolution laid down to that point. It may be said that it calls for a great deal of work and that it imposes an unnecessary burden upon the Government; but it is a wise and sane statement to make, that the Government of the country, or any other country situated as we are, should have the greatest possible knowledge of the food supply of the country and that then it should know where it is going. The other phases which follow in the resolution are not necessarily the consequences of the first positive assertion, although they seem to be taken by the mover of the resolution as necessary consequences of it. I do not think that because the Government knows what quantity of foodstuffs there is in the country and their destination, the prices of foodstuffs will be regulated. I do not know much about the movement of wheat; but as far as I understand commercial conditions in this country, I know of nothing that would prevent a combine of speculators from buying up all the wheat that we have for sale in Canada, taking it to the United States and sending it to our enemies in the old land. This may be an absurd statement to make; but I know of nothing to prevent German money from coming into the United States, with which an American company may be formed for the purpose of buying our wheat and ship-35
ping it to Germany, if it can be got in there.

Germany has
no money.

My hon. friend is an
authority on most things, but I would not care to change my mind with regard to voting for this resolution, because, as he says, there is no money in Germany. I would not care to take the risk of leaving our wheat within easy reach of Germany, even supposing that country has no money.
It is a fair and reasonable proposition that any country that is at war-and we are at war-should have absolute knowledge of tlie sinews of war within its bounds, and that it should have absolute control of where they shall go and how they shall go.
During the session of 1914, when we were only talking about war, which we then deemed to >be far distant, legislation was passed giving control over the export of petroleum oil, because if war broke out, we should have absolute control of the oil so that it should not go out of the country except where thought advisable. If it were right to do that-and the legislation was passed without any controversy-surely it cannot be said that it would be wrong for the Government to have enabling legislation passed at this session to give it power to deal with this wheat question, if it were necessary to do so.
I do not quite understand that it is using very extraordinary powers for the Government of any country to take control of the food supply in time of war. It would be a species of expropriation of property. . Wheat is property and land is property, and I do not think it would be any more drastic to expropiate wheat than to expropriate land.
Does the hon. gentleman not recognize the fact that in so far as the House can give that power, the legislation is already on the statute book?

I am not saying
whether it is on the statute book or not. In reference to wheat, I am not aware that It is. Perhaps the hon. Solicitor-General will tell me where we have such legislation.
In section 6 of the War Measures Act of the session of last August-

It is quite possible. In that case, it is not necessary to legislate; it is a question as to whether it is a wise policy for the Government to act upon the legislation already on the statute book. It does not change the position that I have



taken, which is simply this, that if we exercise the power contained in the 6th section of the statute passed as our War Act of last session, it is ' a certain species of expropriation :	it would be
expropriating wheat instead of, as in other cases, expropriating land. I suppose that it was under that War Act that we expropriated the land at Valcartier. We not only expropriated the land there, but also the grain, the potatoes, and I suppose the cattle in the field. We took everything there was. Surely, if we were justified in doing that, if that was a wise and proper policy, I cannot see that it can be over drastic or unwise to give the Government control of the wheat supply of this country, provided that the owner gets a fair and proper price for it. In view of the suggestion that has been made, what strikes me as possible to happen is that the wheat might go out of the country, and go beyond the border and we not -have anything to say about it. If that happened, I think we should be sorry that we had not adopted laws and regulations to prevent it. I do not think it at all an unreasonable thing to regulate prices of food if a few people are in command of the food of the country and by reason of that food we find that the prices are going up by leaps and bounds.
Speaking for the pait of the country from which I come, the province of Nova Scotia, which is an agricultural country to some extent, also a lumbering, a fishing and perhaps more than anything else, an iron, steel and coal producing country, there are thousands of men there who are dependent for the support of themselves and their families on their day's work. It is a well known fact that for the last eighteen months or more times have been very poor and workmen have not been able to earn the usual amount of money. It is a regrettable fact that it is difficult for these men to feed themselves and their families. It is a startling and discouraging thing for a man who is not earning at all or who is earning but a small wage, and who has seven or eight children to feed, to find that he must pay $9.15 for a barrel of flour. If there is anything the Prime Minister can do to enable that man to pay what is fair and reasonable for flour, and I mention that solely as an example of other things, to see to it that this barrel is sold at a fair profit, so that the farmer will be well paid'' and everybody handling the business well paid, and yet the poor man who buys it will not be robbed, I do not think that, as
	'
guardian of the interests of the people he would be doing anything but what was fair and right. I had the pleasure of hearing the Minister of Finance address a delegation with regard to the price of tobacco. He described the Government on that occasion as the physician of the body politic. I do not find fault with the figure, although I say that the present gang of doctors should never have passed the board and been licensed, still, having been licensed and passed as physicians, they are now in charge of the body politic. And if they now find the body politic suffering with a disease such as hunger, is it not right, from the minister's own definition of his position, that the Government should cause him to take such necessary steps to deal with the disease and reduce such ills as his extraordinary skill in such matters may well bring about? If without injury to the farmer we can keep the somebody who is increasing the prices from doing so, if we can regulate prices so that they should be fair to the poor man, I think that is what this resolution aims at. I do not think that the bon. gentleman is trying to make political capital out of it.
Perhaps I may be pardoned if I go back to somewhat ancient days. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) is fond of quoting history, and he quotes it well, and his comparisons are not always to the advantage of the present day. If we go far back in history we find an instance of a wise man taking control of the wheat of the country. We find him storing it up and selling it out as it suited him. He sold it at proper prices. On another historic occasion there were in the wilderness a tremendous body of men, women and children-twelve thousand. And there was nothing for them to eat except certain small fishes and few loaves of bread. Here was a grand occasion when one man had a corner in the food supply We do not find that the Master told him: This is your chance, my boy; put up your food for sale and you can make your fortune. No, the Regulator and Governor took charge of the whole business. He disposed of the'loaves and fishes, and disposed of them properly. If there is only a little bread and fish to be divided, then those who are responsible for the management of the country should take charge of that food and see to it that it is properly divided so that the country from one end to the other shall be supplied with food so far as that food will go. In my own country, I am sorry to say, the rapid increase in

the price of flour is very embarrassing. When the mines are working, when people can readily sell timber, when the farmers are producing, no particular regulation is necessary. The miner, when he is at work, is a fine customer. In fact he is a little too free with his money, and when the hard times come he is up against it in a very short time.
If this resolution will put power into the hands of the Government that will enable them to say to those who grow wheat that they must not go too high in price, or say to the miller that he must not ask too much for flour, I shall be glad to support it. I have not examined the Bill we passed last August, nor am I suggesting the kind ot legislation we should pass. I am glad to hear the statement of the. Solicitor General that no legislation is necessary because the Government already have the power. That being so, there is no excuse on the part of the Government for not taking action if action is necessary. If this resolution goes to a vote, I shall have no hesitation in voting for it, so far as it goes to carry out the idea that the Government shall know how much food is in the country and where it goes.

It was expected that during the past six months the Government would take some steps to prevent the undue enhancement of the price of foodstuffs; it was confidently asserted in the Government press that such action would be taken by the Government. I did think that the legislation which was passed at the August session of Parliament empowered the Government to take such action, and I quite agree that no further legislation is necessary. It is well known that the price of foodstuffs has been enhanced very far beyond the cost of the ingredients that enter into their production. I saw in the press a few weeks ago a statement that the Bakers' Association of Toronto had made representations to the Minister of Trade and Commerce protesting against the undue increase in the price of the materials entering into the manufacture of their products. It was alleged that the price of these articles had increased by 100 per cent within the last twelve months, and that of this increase the farmers had received only one-tenth.
I think that the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) does not necessarily imply that the farmers should not receive the very best price that they can obtain for their pro-35*
ducts; it is aimed, I think, more particularly, against the middleman, who is taking advantage of existing conditions for the purpose of exacting undue profits. Immediately after war was declared the price of flour in the province of Nova Scotia jumped up $2 a barrel. There was no reason for that increase; the merchants had laid in a stock of flour before war conditions could possibly have affected the price of wheats Nevertheless, without any justification, they added $2, and in some cases more, to the-price of each barrel of flour. I think that is a condition of affairs that ought to be promptly dealt with by the Government. I do not say that the farmers themselves derive too great a profit from their labour and the products of their labour, but I do say that before these products of the farm reach the consumer, the middlemen, through greed and a want of proper appreciation of the unfortunate conditions that confront the labouring men in Canada to-day, unduly increase their profits in respect of these articles. This is applicable to other food products as well as to flour and wheat. I do think that under the circumstances the Government ought not to hesitate to take such steps as would prevent the undue increase in the price of foodstuffs by the middlemen.

The matter of handling wheat in Canada has always been a vexed question, but in my opinion the most important consideration with which we are now confronted is that of seeing that the farmers in western Canada particularly those in the drouth-stricken districts, are supplied with seed grain. I understand that the Interior Department, under the arrangements which they have made, can supply only 400 bushels to each farmer, while many farmers in western Canada need 1,000 or 2,000 bushels of wheat for seed purposes. Some arrangement should be made whereby these farmers can be supplied with the necessary amount of seed grain. I think the Government would be justified in amending the banking laws of Canada so that banks would be empowered to take seed grain mortgages- which they can not do under the present law-thus enabling them to help the [DOT] western farmers to obtain the extra seed grain that they need.
The great difficulty in connection with the wheat question is not the prices the farmers have been getting, but the extent to which the middlemen, or the millers, boost prices after 90 per cent of the wheat leaves the farmers' hands. Ever since I

have been in western Canada the dealers and the millers have manipulated the prices and the market so that the producer of the grain receives the very lowest price and the consumer pays the very highest. Every year a special train leaves Winnipeg with millers, grain dealers and reporters; they travel over the prairie, and when they get back they spread abroad reports of the great crop we are going to have in western Canada. In this manner they pound the price down to the very lowest possible point; then the moment the wheat is sold by the farmer they start a cry about the great shortage of crop-that it will not be nearly as large as expected. Up, then, goes the price to the consumer, and the toll is paid to the middlemen.
Some persons say: why do the farmers not hold the wheat? Because the farmers *owe money to the loan companies, machinery companies and general stores; these accounts must be paid, and they are compelled to sell their grain to obtain the necessary funds. The crop of 1913 was sold by the farmers at an average price of 65 cents a bushel. It costs over 60 cents to grow a bushel of grain, so hon. gentlemen can see that the farmers of western Canada made no money out of that crop. In the past year 90 per cent of the wheat went out of the farmers' hands at an average price of from 80 cents to $1 a bushel, and to-day it is boosted up to $1.65. I submit that this Government should control the gambling in the food products of Canada. To-day a man can go on the option market and buy wheat on a three cent margin. I think we should pass some law whereby speculators would be obliged to pay a margin of 25 cents on each bushel of wheat they buy. This would do away with a gi'eat deal of speculation in wheat. I have no hesitation in saying that in my opinion the middlemen-in this case the millers and the grain-dealers-are the persons who are robbing the people of this country. They rob the farmer, the man who grows the wheat, and they rob the consumer as well. The farmers of western Canada have 13,000,000 acres ready for wheat for next spring. If we have an average crop of 20 bushels to the acre, that will mean 260,000,000 bushels * of wheat grown in the prairie provinces for next year. Some 60,000,000 bushels of wheat will be sufficient for bread and seed for the three provinces, which will leave 200,000,000 bushels for export. So that even before we started this great cry of patriotism and production the farmers of western Canada were getting ready to supply the old country markets. I think that it would be a mistake 
for this Government to try to control the price of wheat, but I do think they should control the gambling in the food products of this country.

I wish to offer a few remarks on this motion. I would not have done so, but apparently there are at least three hon. members in this House who are in sympathy with the resolution. When you allow your imagination to picture the vast extent of this country and our great community of interest, I do not think that you can come to any other conclusion than that this resolution is narrow and provincial in its character. It is an attempt to interfere with legitimate business, and would, as Premier Asquith stated with regard to similar legislation in the old land, cause no end of trouble.
Most of the discussion here to-day has reference to the effect that the resolution would have on the farmers of western Canada. The jnover of it, however, conies * from the province of Ontario. We do a little farming in the province of Ontario. Of course, the farmers there are not just as up to date as they are in other parts of the country, but this resolution would affect them to some extent at least; and I am sure that when the farmers of Canada read in the papers to-morrow the discussion that took place here on a resolution of this kind, they will be very much amused to think that this House has devoted as much time as it has to a discussion of this nature. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. W. H. Sharpe) thinks that the Government should not limit the amount of seed to be advanced to the western farmer to 400 bushels, that some farmers will require 1,000 or 2,000 bushels. I think that any farmer who has sufficient land to require 2,000 bushels to seed it, that is, 1,000 acres, should be in a position to acquire seed for himself without any assistance from the Government. I do not think it is a good thing for any clas's in a community to expect the Government to take up every little scheme and to solve all difficulties for them. I do not believe that that is in accordance with the genius of our people, nor do I think it would result in any benefit to them. I quite agree that the homesteader who may have invested every dollar he had in securing funds to work his homestead and who may have land ready for seed, if he is not in a position to procure seed, should have it advanced to him, as the Government in such case has ample security for the money advanced.

I wish to tell the House some-
9 p.m. thing about the western farmers.
I have heard so much in the House and outside of it about the farmers in Eastern Canada advising the farmers in the West w'hat to do, that I shall not advise them at all, as I do not feel competent to do so; nor am I going to advise the farmers in Ontario; hut I want to tell some of the western farmers what some farmers in western Ontario are doing. They are buying stock in the West, shipping it down here to Ontario and buying feed from other parts of the country and from the United States; they are feeding that stock and putting it on the market, and they are doing that year after year. They are not doing that just for the fun of the thing, but they are doing it from a business standpoint. Two feed merchants in the constituency I represent have sold during the present winter nineteen carloads of cotton seed meal to be fed to stock in that county. This is a feature of Ontario farming. In the West farming is supposed to be wheat growing, but this resolution covers a great deal more than the growing of wheat. It has been read a number of times, but I shall read part of it again:
That, in the opinion of this House, the circumstances arising out of the present war are such as to justify the Government of Canada in exercising supreme control over the quantity and destiny of our food exports, thereby regulating the prices at which bread, meat and other food products shall be sold for home consumption.
I am satisfied that agriculture cannot be carried on in this country, ot in any other country, without stock raising being an adjunct of it, or rather, the basis on which it is founded. We found lately a change in the price of cattle in the cattle markets. I quote from the Toronto Globe of February 18:
The bottom fell yesterday out of the beef cattle market in Toronto, and it may take a little while to restore it. Various causes are given for the almost unprecedented drop in prices, but only one of them seems to have in it any element of permanency: scarcity and consequent dearness of fodder. The combination of this with other causes has produced a situation which is by no means pleasant to pass through, but which is not likely to last very long. It would be a mistake for cattle-owners to hasten to get rid of their stock for fear of a worse thing happening to them; better far hold the animals over even at an undue cost, and take chances of a better market with improved cattle.
We have a solution offered here for the high cost of living in this country. A commission was appointed a year ago to investigate the high cost of living in Canada. The Globe undertakes to solve the beef question, and I shall read its solution:
If it be said there are no lands fit for cattle-ranching purposes the answer must be that there are such lands in abundance in Northern Ontario. The obstacle to be overcome is not the lack of suitable land, but the unreasoning though apparently invincible skepticism of the beef cattle producers. Wherever the deer can live and thrive in a state of nature cattle can live and thrive with a little factitious assistance, and on a woodland ranch they will cost less and thrive better, even in winter, than if housed up and tended with great labour in the most new-fashioned subterranean stables.
We have not yet had a resolution before the House with regard to the land now occupied toy the deer. Possibly something of that nature will develop before very long.
The farmers of Ontario to-day are feeding their livestock at a great loss, yet you never hear a word offered in this House or outside of it in sympathy with them. People are very ready to advise the farmer what to do. We have at the present time a movement on foot throughout Canada called the " patriotism and production campaign." I Shall not say very much about that, but personally I believe that if these gentlemen would devote-their energies to prayer, they might accomplish just as much as they will accomplish by what they are doing. The farmers of Canada are just as alive to their own interests as any other class in the community, and possibly not any more so. I cannot see any reason why they should be singled out at a time like this, as distinguished from any other time, to be made victims for the benefit of others. We have a community of interests in this country, anc^ if we are going to make of Canada a country such as we hope to make it, there must be times when some sections or communities must suffer while others will be in a position to reap greater benefits. I am sorry that the matter has been taken so seriously by the House. I did not think there was any occasion for it and I am satisfied that the mover of the resolution did not fully consider the matter before bringing it to the attention of the House. As far as the farmers of Ontario are concerned- and they have just as great interests at stake as any other section of Canada- they are not asking for special favours, yet they do not want to be hampered in their legitimate business.
I believe that the greatest difficulty that the farmers have to contend with is the transportation problem and the lack of

labour on the farm. These two things have brought about conditions that are detrimental to the whole country. We hear about thousands being out of employment in the towns and cities. No doubt many of them cannot get away from those places; all they have is invested there, they own their houses probably, they are mechanics and they are not accustomed to any other work. In the cities of Ontario there never was a time when it was more difficult to get men to go out and work upon the farm. That has been the case during the whole winter and I repeat that it was never more difficult to get men to work on the farms in Ontario than at the preseent time. That is the position. I went into the immigration office in the city of Toronto on Saturday last and the man in charge there said: Nothing doing here; I just placed one man last week. What do you think of that? Yet the cities are feeding thousands of men who say they cannot get employment in this country. Mind you, this is during the winter months. Some people say: Why does not the farmer build a house on the farm and keep his men the year round? These men will not stay with the farmer more than eight or nine months and then they flock to the cities. If many of the large cities would only exercise proper control over the unemployed they would not find so many people asking for assistance.
The condition that has come about in this country has developed during the last few years. When the farmers got to the stage when protection was of some value to them we found then, and not until then, that the Government of the day were prepared to allow imports of food products into this country free of duty. It was not- until then that the conditions of which I am speaking manifested themselves. The farmers turned down that proposition and if you look over the imports into this country during the past few years you will find that we have in Canada a market that is second to none in the world. If we just leave things as they are and do not meddle with them we will find that a greater number will be induced to go back to the land and a greater development will take place in Canada than has been the case for many years past. I do not think that we need worry about this proposition. Let us see if we can improve the transportation facilities of this country, and I must say that I do not look very hopefully on the prospect. I see great obstacles in the way of doing that. We have altogether too many duplications of trans-

portation facilities for what we have to transport and the result is that it will be impossible to give us the rate that we would have had if we did not have so many transcontinental lines.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (South Cape Breton) :
speechtext:
If I correctly understand the resolution as proposed by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt), I am in perfect accord with it. My understanding of it is that the Government should take some steps to prohibit the enormous profit that middlemen are making upon the food products of the country. It is proposed, as I understand it, that the Government should take some steps to control the foodstuffs of the country, especially flour, wheat and the items mentioned in the resolution. I could well imderstand the sentiment of the last speaker (Mr. Sutherland) if the farmers were making some of the enormous profits which are being made, and have been made, on foodstuffs since June, July and August of last year. My thon. friend -says that the resolution is too marrow and provincial. I take a somewhat different view. I believe that this resolution is calculated to bring to the attention of the Government a serious grievance which the consumers have at the present time. He says that the proposal of the resolution is to make the farmers the victims. The farmers are the victims already. That was pointed out by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. W. H. Sharpe). I would not have any hesitation about expressing the wish that the farmers should get the very best prices they could for -the products of their farms. I would like to see the fishermen and miners getting the very best prices they could for the products of their labour. When these products are cornered by middlemen and speculators, or when products of the farm are cornered by perhaps half a dozen speculators, who hoard them in their granaries, the products of the western farms, as well as the products of the eastern farms and the farms of Ontario, when they take advantage of the misfortune of Canada, in common with the rest of the Empire, in connection with the struggle which we are waging, to force consumers to pay exorbitant and, I might -say, awful prices for their food, it is the duty of the Government, in the interests of the people, to do something that shall prevent these middlemen, these speculators, from making fortunes themselves at the expense of the common people and of the Empire at large.
What is the fact? When we are buying flour in western Canada for $6 a barrel the

farmer on the prairie was making as much money as he is to-day. The farmer, three, four and five years ago, when we in the East were paying $6 and sometimes $5.75 a barrel for the very best flour, was making as much money as he is to-day. Wbat are we paying in eastern Canada for flour? We are paying $9.25 for Five Roses flour, a brand which, I understand, is made from hard w^eat. I do not think that the farmers in the West are making any more money on account of the excessive rise in the price of flour which has taken place during the past three or four months than they were making before. I have been given to understand by many people from western Canada that the wheat of the farmers of the West was sold to the millers and middlemen at not very much over the ordinary rate and that the middlemen and millers took advantage of the misfortunes of the country. We pride ourselves on being loyal to the Empire, and I think it is a proud boast that we are trying to do everything we can to further the interests of our common Empire in this struggle for existence. To-day the wheat market in Canada and the price of the wheat that we are exporting to the old land are controlled by the Chicago market, a market which is foreign to the British Empire. I can point to several milling industries in this country whose stocks have increased eight points since last Christmas, and of course the farmers who raised the wheat derive no profit from that. We have in the world to-day plenty of wheat and plenty of flour for consumption until the next crop is harvested, but it is not supply and demand which controls the price, but speculators who have hoarded the produce of the world and who are waxing fat at the expense of the Canadian and British taxpayer and consumer. The Government would be doing only its duty if it enforced the legislation passed at the special session of Parliament in August. The hon. gentleman suggested that it is possible that some of our wheat has reached the markets of our enemies, and indeed the public press of this country has made the statement that Canadian wheat has been shipped to the United States and thence to enemies' ports. I have no evidence to corroborate that, but if it be so it is all the more reason why the Government should take control of the flour and wheat remaining in this country.
I would not be so pronounced in favour of the idea set out in the resolution, if the workers in the industrial centres of Canada were living under the same conditions as
they were a year ago. In eastern Canada, and that is the only portion of Canada as to which I am thoroughly familiar with the conditions, our operators in the mines and steel plants are working now about half time, and it is an enormous hardship on those who are only earning half the ordinary wages that they should have to pay almost double for the flour, the meat and the bread, which are necessaries of their subsistence. It is not very often I am able to agree with the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), but in this case I endorse most heartily his suggestion that the Government should exercise control over the price and the export of Canadian foodstuffs. This is not the only parliament in which this question is now being discussed. I have no doubt that in a day or two we shall get a very pronounced idea from the Government and Parliament of Great Britain as to what they intend to do with regard to this question. The last reports I have seen in our newspapers, and also in a newspaper published in Sydney, Australia, was that the Australasian Government intended to take over control of practically all the foodstuffs in that country. If it were that the farmers or producers were being made the victoms in not getting a reasonable price for their products, I would not raise my voice in favour of this resolution, but we know that such is not the fact. The wheat has gone from the farmers and they have only received a reasonable price for it, so that the people who are getting these exorbitant profits are the speculators and the middlemen who never ploughed a furrow or garnered an ear of wheat. I believe that the Government will be well advised, should they exercise the power they have and control the prices of foodstuffs, as well as the export of wheat and flour from this country, so that it cannot reach channels where it may become the staff of life of the enemies of the Empire.

speechtext:
One hon. member on the other side of the House suggested that the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), in proposing this resolution, desired to east some reflection upon the patriotism of the farmers of Canada. I am bound to say that I gathered no such idea or meaning from anything said by the hon. member for Brantford. I know that he realizes, as all members of the House realize, the spirit of patriotism which has inspired the farmers of Canada, whether in the East or in the West, and all the people of Canada, in the great crisis which the Empire now faces. I desire to join in

the appreciation which has been expressed by an hon. gentleman on the other side, of the spirit of those citizens who have come to us from the south of the line, and who, at the present time, as indeed before the war broke out, are discharging in the most commendable manner all the duties of Canadian citizenship.
An hon. gentleman on the other side of the House suggested that my hon. friend from Brantford and those in his community, should be prepared to make some sacrifice themselves. I would like that hon. gentleman to bear in mind that the hon. memoer for Brantford is making the greatest of all sacrifices that a man can make,, in sending those of his own family and. his own flesh and blood to fight fot the Empire.
I deeply regret, as every hon. member regrets, that there are workingmen in Brantford, and doubtless in other industrial centres, who at the present time are not able to find employment to the full extent they would desire, but there is the consideration that conditions in Canada are certainly not worse in that respect, and perhaps not so bad, as tney are in the neighbouring republic. We know from statements appearing in the press of the United States that this war has brought about conditions there perhaps more depressing than anything to which we can point in this country at the present time; but, as far as those men in Canada who lack work at the moment are concerned, it would be more in the general interest, more in the interest of the men themselves, that we should endeavour to turn our energies, so far as the Government may exercise any power at its command, to find some means of providing work for them rather than to undertake the control of the price of food supplies, except under certain conditions to which I will allude a little later on.
I am very glad indeed to hear my hon. friend the member for Brantford say that a certain manufacturing company with which he is understood to be associated has not increased, and does not intend to increase, the price of its products to the farmers or other persons in this country who may desire to purchase them. The allusion made by one hon. gentleman on the other side of the House as to some increase in price in that regard can not have any relation to that company, or to other companies in a similar line of business who are manufacturing in Canada at the present time.
So far as the general question is con-f*s:r Robert Borden.]
cerned, the policy which the Government has endeavoured to follow since the outbreak of war is not to interfere with the business activities of the country, except in so far as this is absolutely and imperatively demanded of it by reason of the war or by reason of conditions arising out of the war. In other words, the less interference by a Government under conditions such as prevail at the present time, the less interference with the business activities of the country, with the sale or the free interchange of products, the better for the country, except in so far as the war itself demands otherwise. If my hon. friend from Brantford had found it convenient to come to myself or to some other member of the Government for information on some points on which he has addressed the House this . afternoon, he might have saved himself the trouble of making some points of his speech. He has spoken in the first place of the desirability of regulating the export of food products, particularly wheat. He has spoken in the second place of the desirability of regulating the destination of such food products, particularly wheat, so that they shall not reach an enemy country. In the third place, he has spoken of the desirability of regulating the price at which such food products should he sold in this country.
Let us take, in the first place, the question of export. That presents itself to us in two aspects: firstly, the desirability of preventing any such export as would leave the people of this country destitute, between now and the next harvest, of a sufiicient food supply. I would like to point out to my hon. friend that the question of food supply, so far as wheat and wheat products are concerned, is not solely a question of the wheat in this country, but a question of the wheat available for milling and of the'flour in the country. I would like to assure him and all other hon. members that this subject has more or less engaged the attention of the Government; that we know something of the supply in that regard, and that we do not think conditions in this country at the present time are such as to make any action by the Government necessary so far as that particular feature of the question is concerned.
In the next place, my hon. friend speaks of wheat leaving this country and reaching an enemy country. In that is involved the question of destination, to which I alluded a moment ago. He has spoken of a return which has been brought down, and he has attached importance to the fact that 368 barrels of flour seem to have reached Germany since the first day of August last.

Every lion, member knows that since the proclamation, which has been validated by Parliament, it is absolutely impossible for any man in this country to have intercourse by way of trade with any citizen of an enemy country, unless he desires to place himself under very severe penalties of the law. Therefore, I would assume that the 368 barrels-which seems a very minor matter to be alarmed about-must have gone between the first and the fourth of August; because my hon. friend asked for a return from the first of August, and there was no declaration of war until the evening of the fourth of August. So far as the exports to Holland and Norway are concerned, they do not seem to be very much greater than those which took place in ordinary years. If my hon- friend had directed his attention to the Canada Gazette, he would have found an important enactment by the Government in that regard, to which I will, in a moment, draw the attention of the House.
With regard to the question of prohibiting export from this country of any article of supply which might be useful to the enemy, we have acted thoroughly in accordance with a committee constituted for that purpose in Great Britain, whose activities commenced almost immediately after the war had begun-a committee which deals almost entirely with the question of prohibiting or not prohibiting the export from Great Britain, or, by co-operation with the Government of any Dominion, from any British possession, of articles which may be of use to the enemy. On occasions when recommendations or suggestions have come to us, we have felt called upon, in the interests of this Dominion, to make certain representations to the committee through the British Government which have always been met in the most friendly spirit, and there has always been friendly co-operation in all such matters between the Government of the United Kingdom and the Government of Canada from the very first. So far as this particular question is concerned, there has never been the slightest difference between the two Governments, and the suggestions of the Government of the United Kingdom have never been called in question by us, nor has our action ever been called in question by it. In accordance with the suggestions of that committee communicated to us, we passed an Order in Council on the 29th day of October last by which we prohibited the exportation from Canada of certain articles to all foreign ports in Europe and on the Mediterranean and Black seas,
with the exception of those of France, Russia (except the Baltic ports), Spain and Portugal. Among the articles enumerated, in a long list with which I need not trouble the House, I find feeding stuffs for animals and all foodstuffs and raw materials for the same. Therefore I desire to assure my hon. friend and all hon. members that this subject has been taken into consideration in the first place by the British Government, and especially by the committee to which I have just now alluded, and, in the second place, upon representations and suggestions from the committee through taie British Government, by the Government of Canada, with the result which I have just now pointed out.
In the next place, my hon. friend suggests that there should be a regulation of the price of foodstuffs, more particularly of wheat. So far as wheat is concerned, I would be very sorry to attempt anything of the kind, and for the following reasons. In the first place, the price of wheat, as has been recognized in this House and in the country ever since I have been a member of the House, is regulated by the markets of the world, regulated very largely by the prices established in the great markets of the Mother Country. Now, if we undertook to regulate the price, what would be a fair basis for doing so? A fair basis would be to regulate it from time to time in accordance with what would be determined by the markets of the world. For, inasmuch as the farmer, when the price of wheat is low, must be limited in the price which he receives by the markets of the world from time to time, in common justice we can only adopt the same principle when the price has been increased by exceptional conditions, and that would leave the matter where it was in the first place. For us to say to the farmer, when the price of wheat is at the highest by -reason of war or other conditions, that we must limit the price which he receives, and that in other years and under other conditions he must accept a price which barely covers what it costs him to grow the wheat, that would seem to me a position which could not be maintained. At all events, it is a position which I would not care to take, nor is it one to which I could give my sanction. Therefore I do not think it would be desirable for the country to attempt any such course as my hon. friend has suggested. We desire in this country that there shall be more production from the land. It would

be, I think, a very unfortunate initiative on the part of this Government to undertake at the present time and under present conditions the limitation of the price which the farmer shall receive for his wheat.
That leads to quite another aspect of the situation, and that is, the efforts of people in this country to combine for the purpose of raising the price of foodstuffs after they have left the hands of the first producers. We have not been unmindful of our duty in that regard, and have endeavoured to watch the situation very carefully. A great many representation of a general character have been made to me from time to time, and if any good ground can be established to show that people are combining for the purpose of enhancing unduly the prices of foodstuffs in a general way throughout Canada, I am bound to say that the Government would feel it its duty to give consideration to these representations, and to determine whether or not some action should be taken in the early future.
So far as foodstuffs are concerned, the hon. gentleman has only spoken of wheat, flour and meat. I am not disposed, from the information before me at the present moment, to agree that the prices of meat products have advanced. _ My information is that not only has there been a reduction in the prices of some of these products there are many food products in Canada as to which there is a difficulty in finding a market. During the past two or three months we have been endeavouring to find markets in the United Kingdom for food products, which may spoil for lack of people to consume them. For example, there is an enormous quantity of canned goods for which there is the greatest difficulty in securing materials even at cost prices. I understand from my colleague from the province of New Brunswick, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), that in that province there is a surplus of potatoes of about a million and a half bushels for which they would be glad to find a market. We know there has been a great abundance of apples. And we know that at one time-though not so much lately-there was considerable difficulty apprehended in finding a market for the surplus fish product of the country. I understand the situation in that regard has been improved in the last few weeks. So that I cannot see that there is any special reason for us to pass the resolution 
my hon. friend from Brantford has proposed.
I have listened to what my hon. friend from Brantford has said as' to the danger to the Mother Country of a lack of food supplies. I can only say that if there is any such danger apprehended in the Mother Country at the present time, I have given ample notice within the last six or eight weeks of very great stores of food supplies which the producers of this country would be very glad to send to the United Kingdom at not more than they have cost them, without any profit. So I do not think we need have much apprehension so far as the Mother Country is concerned. The authorities of the United Kingdom, if there were any danger or difficulty in that regard, would have found occasion to communicate with us in reply to our frequent communications as to available stores in Canada. On the contrary, when we have communicated with them on the subject, they have in almost every case assured us that there were large stores of the particular articles in question available in the United Kingdom. Naturally, they would be glad indeed to assist us, if they could do so, in finding a market in the United Kingdom for the surplus food products of Canada, but they were not needed there at that moment.
Under the circumstances, while I appreciate the motive of my hon. friend from Brantford in bringing the matter to the attention of the Government, I regret that we cannot find it desirable to accept the motion at the moment. If conditions should at a later day so develop as to make anything of the kind necessary, my hon. friend may feel quite sure that we shall endeavour to keep in very close touch with the situation and take such measures as, according to our understanding of the conditions, may be necessary for the purpose he has in mind.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew) : I had intended making a few remarks before the Prime Minister spoke. I had not the pleasure of hearing all'my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) said on this question. I think the importance of the question entitles it to considerable attention on the part of the House, because people throughout Canada are talking about this matter a good deal. The trouble is that nobody seems to have a real cure for it. I am inclined to agree with the Prime Minister that the great strength of

the British Empire at the present time is that she with her Dominions has plenty of foodstuffs. However long this war may last there will be foodstuffs enough to see the Empire through. So far as the products of our Canadian people are concerned, I do not foresee any danger. As to prices and the high cost of living, I had hoped that the report of the commission appointed by the Government would have been down before this, so that we could have seen what was the cause and what should be the cure. The difficulty seems to be with us in Canada, as elsewhere, that cheap prices to the producer do not always mean cheap prices to the consumer. Between the price received by the man behind the plough and the price paid by the man who consumes the product there is too wide a spread to be accounted for by an ordinary profit, it is argued. I would not say we should not have middlemen. "Middleman" is merely another name for a dealer in articles of commerce. Properly conducted, this is as honourable a business as a man can follow. The business of the world could not be systematically conducted if it were not for the operation of specialists who go between, as it were, other individuals or bodies who are hot specialists. It may be that in Canada there are too many people who handle the goods between the time they are produced and the time they are consumed; I had hoped that the commission of investigation would look into that phase of the question, and, perhaps, have thrown some light upon it. Again, there may be many middlemen who are anxious to make two or three profits; that is human nature, and you will almost have to remodel man before you altogether eradicate that from his system. The man, however, who will take advantage of the patriotism of the people and their loyal devotion to king and country in order to fill his own pockets is the worst kind of traitor that can be found; he is trading on the best that is in people for his own selfish purposes. As to whether that could be controlled, I am not prepared to say; in any case I am inclined-to think that it could not be controlled in the manner suggested by the hon. member for Brantford. It is a big question, and could not be grappled with in a few moments.
Tire question of unemployment is one that comes very close to those who live in industrial centres, large or small. Although many persons are out of employment at present, I think I am safe in saying that in many of our manufacturing centres men
have employment to-day that they would not have had if there had been no war. A. great many of our factories-I speak from personal knowledge-aTe working half-time, some three-quarter time, some full time and some double time, on orders which they have obtained as a result of the war.
I touch now upon a very delicate point: I was severely criticised for referring to this at several patriotic meetings which I addressed throughout Canada. Without going into what I consider to be the duty of the banks at the present time, I submit that it is as important to the British Empire that the whistles should ibe kept blowing everywhere as it is that men should be kept in the trenches. Anything that does not tend to accomplish this does not tend to the best interests of Canada and the Empire as a whole. I think it is fair to the manufacturing interests to say that they have manufactured goods in many instances to the full capacity of their warehouses. They have no sale for the goods; many of them have stock on hand sufficiently large to last a year or more, and unless they have new capital they are not in a position to engage in further manufactures. I think the banks ought to do all they can to enable the manufacturers to go on manufacturing and putting their goods in the warehouse until such time as they cah be sold. That would give employment to the men-if not permanently, at least for a time-and thus remove from the people of Canada and from the Empire as well, one of the greatest difficulties which we now have to face. It has been charged that the banks are not as generous as they should be. I am not sufficiently expert in financial matters to critcise them in that respect, but it does strike me that now is the time, if ever -there was a time, when the financial. institutions ought to take full advantage of the privileges given them by the Government and to do their utmost to see that the manufacturing establishments of Canada are kept going as near full time as possible. That would reduce the seriousness of the unemployment question to a minimum, at least.
I am fearful lest some of our mineral productions may possibly get into the hands of the enemy; I speak now more particularly of our nickel and copper. It has been said that the British Government is perfectly satisfied that none of it is getting into the hands of the enemy, and I am glad of that assertion. The Dominion of Canada, a part of the Britisn Empire, and France, one of her Allies, control practi-

cally the whole nickel output of the world. With the supply from these sources shut off, it is only a matter of mathematical calculation as to how long Germany can find an adequate supply of this material to carry on her warfare. I think it is absolutely important and in the interests of the Allies that we should be perfectly sure that not an ounce of our copper or nickel gets to Germany. She can get her wheat elsewhere, but she cannot get her copper and nickel elsewhere than from the Allies. I hope everything has been done that can be done to this end; if anything can be done by the Government to make it absolutely impossible for our nickel to get into the hands of the enemy, I am prepared to support any steps that they may take to that end. I would not go so far as some hon. gentlemen propose and forbid the export of nickel for all time to come, but I would urge on the Government that all possible precautions be taken to prevent its getting into the hands of the enemy. I am far more concerned about that than I am about the food supply, because I think that under the circumstances, if there are not too many go-betweens operating between the producer and the consumer, supply and demand will usually regulate the prices.

So I might go on and quote the remarks of many statesmen who ha<re given attention to this subject and have thought it well worthy to discuss and give consideration to. Further, I pointed out that Australia, a country quite as democratic as ours, a country ruled by the labour party at the present time, did not wait very long for the action of Parliament. They did not take into consideration all that might happen in the first six months of the war, but in about one month after the war began the Government of Australia took possession of the wheat supply of Australia and arbitrarily fixed the price at $1.25 per bushel. In my judgment they took a wise action. New Zealand is in the same position. Every country in Europe, bar Russia, is short of food. Some are in that position to-day; they have no food at present and no prospects for the future. Belgium, the best tilled country in the world, has been devastated from end to end and no crop is likely to be put in there during the coming season. Seven million people are dependent upon the outside world for their food supply. Eighty thousand tons of food are required weekly to feed the people of Belgium. What is true of Belgium is also true of Poland, what is true of Poland is true of Serbia, and what is true of Serma is partially true of Austria, Germany and France. Try as we may, we in Canada do not realize what the people of Europe are contending with. They know what the scarcity of food means, they know what it means to go to the cupboard and find no loaf or anything else, with a wife and perishing children in the house. They know the effect of want. They know what it means to lack food and clothing. All these things are denied to many of the people of the nations of Europe who are probably just as much deserving at the hands of Providence as we are in this splendid and comparatively prosperous country.	*
What I have pointed out in this House I have done in all sincerity, believing that I was justified by the statistics that I have quoted. I believe that the food supply of Canada should be conserved, firstly, for the British people themselves, and then for the Allies, and the countries friendly with the Mother Country in the cause that we have espoused. I have not heard that part of the subject challenged very seriously. My right hon. friend the Prime Min-
ister has said that probably this amount of flour that went to Germany was sent there before war was declared. Possibly that is the explanation, but I think the explanation in regard to Norway and Holland that are closely in touch with Germany and I have no doubt have been feeding the Germans to a greater or less extent, may be open to grave doubt.

I do not know
whether I made myself clear to my h>n. friend. On the 29th October last we passed an Order in Council which covered Norway and Holland.

I did not understand my right hon. friend to make that statement. I know there is an Order in Council, but I am not so sure even here to-night that that Order in Council has been quite as effective as it might have been; at least, there is in the mind of some people,, and evidently in that of many newspapers, the idea may be a mistaken one-that some food from Canada has been reaching enemy countries. There is little doubt of that. Only recently seven carloads of flour shipped to Salonika were held up at the border. I give all credit to the head of the department who did it. I do not know who did it but I understand that seven carloads that were just being sent out of Canada three or four weeks ago bound for Salonika, which is part of the enemy's country, were held up. Flour should be consigned to our own Allies if we have any to spare, or should be kept to furnish the sinews of war to our own cause and for our own people and not be diverted into enemy countries.
I have only issued this as a kind of warning. I have been freely criticised. I am ready for criticism in a fair and reasonable way but when I am criticised I would like my hon. friends to show wherein the statistics and figures I have given were contrary to the fact. If they did not vary from the fact then I have made out a case that is worthy of the best consideration of the Government.' I have no desire to make what is hard any harder for any of the hon. gentlemen who are on the treasury benches who are controlling the destinies of this country. Nothing was further from my mind than that any further difficulty should be put upon them, any single ounce of burden that they are not at present bearing because they have plenty upon their shoulders to deal with in these war problems. I have every confidence that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has this matter

under very close survellance and that he is prepared to see that everything I have suggested is done. I am sure that the country will feel that the air has been somewhat cleared at least by the reassuring statement of the Prime Minister and others that we in Canada have no cause to worry, that the British Empire has no cause to worry, that food supplies are in abundance and are likely to be and that we are not likely to suffer from any adversity of that kind. I trust that is true, but I feel that I have done nothing short of my duty, and anything beyond my duty, in endeavouring to point out to the House that in my judgment the amount of our exportation and the destination of it should be under the strict supervision of the Government and that there should at all times be available in this country a supply necessary for our own domestic requirements and that if we h'ave anything over it should be kept for Great Britain and the other overseas dominions.
Under the circumstances, I do not desire to press my motion. I have received considerable support and also a good deal of criticism. I presume that the temper of the House is that it would not be -wise at the present time to pass this resolution and in view of the promise of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, who has stated that they will keep an eye upon the situation and if it becomes necessary will act in so far as speculation at any rate is concerned, I do not think it would be wise for me to challenge a division of the House. Taking what the Prime Minister has said as being likely to happen, and accepting his promise that they will watch this question in such a manner as to see that no injustice is done to anybody in Canada, I leave the matter and will be quite willing for you, Mr. Speaker, to call the resolution "lost upon division."
Motion negatived on division.
